title: EU Taxonomy: General Court largely upholds aviation and shipping criteria
authors: Julia Voskoboinikova, Julia Grothaus, Rachel Barrett, Raza Naeem, Daniella Strik, Guillaume Croisant
description:
On 30 September 2026, the EU General Court ruled on a challenge brought by three environmental NGOs against the technical screening criteria (TSC) for aviation and maritime transport under the EU Taxonomy, adopted by the European Commission in 2023.
The NGOs took the refusal to the EU General Court.
The General Court dismissed almost the entire action.
The Taxonomy criteria for aviation and shipping remain in force and continue to apply.
The Commission must re-open the internal review on that point and is expected to revise the maritime criteria.
text:
On 30 September 2026, the EU General Court ruled on a challenge brought by three environmental NGOs against the technical screening criteria (TSC) for aviation and maritime transport under the EU Taxonomy, adopted by the European Commission in 2023.

The NGOs had asked the Commission to withdraw the criteria allowing certain conventional aircraft and gas-fuelled vessels to count as "transitional" sustainable activities. The Commission refused in June 2024. The NGOs took the refusal to the EU General Court. For more information, see our previous blog post.

The General Court dismissed almost the entire action. It confirmed the Commission's broad discretion under Article 19 of the Taxonomy Regulation. It rejected both aviation pleas, including challenges to the CO2 thresholds, the fleet replacement ratio and the minimum sustainable aviation fuel percentages. It also rejected most of the maritime pleas.

The Court upheld one point of the challenge: for gas-fuelled vessels, a requirement to use "state-of-the-art" methane-slippage mitigation cannot stand on its own. Where verification depends on compliance with emissions thresholds, the criterion must either set those thresholds itself or expressly cross-refer to an identifiable standard (such as FuelEU Maritime). On that basis, the Commission's refusal to re-examine the criteria was annulled to that limited extent.

The Taxonomy criteria for aviation and shipping remain in force and continue to apply. In practice, however, the methane-slippage condition for gas-fuelled vessels should now be read subject to the Court's finding. The Commission must re-open the internal review on that point and is expected to revise the maritime criteria. The timing has not been announced, and an appeal to the Court of Justice on points of law remains open to either side.

title: Bain Capital sees China SAF mandates driving long-term growth in sustainable aviation fuel
description:
His comments come as EcoCeres prepares for a planned initial public offering (IPO) in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong target supports EcoCeres’ expansion plans Bain Capital invested more than $700 million in EcoCeres in 2022.
Its plants in Zhangjiagang in eastern China and Johor in Malaysia have combined renewable fuel production capacity of around 770,000 tonnes annually.
Hong Kong has separately set a target for SAF to account for 1%–3% of fuel used by departing flights by 2030.
The facility is scheduled to begin operations by 2030 and is expected to supply airports in Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou.
text:
Hong Kong: Bain Capital expects government blending mandates across several countries to drive long-term growth in the sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) sector and anticipates that China will introduce such requirements in the coming years, according to a senior executive at the private equity firm, Reuters reported.

James Tam, a partner at Bain Capital and co-chair of SAF producer EcoCeres, said the industry was entering a period of long-term expansion as governments extended rules requiring airlines to reduce carbon emissions from Europe to Asia.

“SAF is almost the only commercially available solution to decarbonise aviation,” Tam said in an interview, adding that hydrogen-powered and electric aircraft were unlikely to become practical alternatives for long-haul flights in the near future.

His comments come as EcoCeres prepares for a planned initial public offering (IPO) in Hong Kong. Reuters reported in September that the company could raise around $1 billion through the offering. Tam declined to comment on the IPO details, which could provide an indication of investor interest in companies focused exclusively on sustainable aviation fuel.

Despite expectations of long-term growth, the sector is facing weak demand and substantial unused production capacity as airlines remain reluctant to pay the higher prices associated with SAF.

The International Air Transport Association said in June that global SAF production was expected to reach 2.4 million tonnes in 2026, equivalent to just 0.8% of global jet fuel demand. The association also projected that production capacity would exceed 9 million tonnes, indicating a gap between available capacity and expected output.

Hong Kong target supports EcoCeres’ expansion plans

Bain Capital invested more than $700 million in EcoCeres in 2022. Tam said EcoCeres was the second company, after Finland’s Neste, to commercialise SAF production.

The company supplies international airlines, including Qantas, Air France, British Airways and Cathay Pacific. Its plants in Zhangjiagang in eastern China and Johor in Malaysia have combined renewable fuel production capacity of around 770,000 tonnes annually.

Tam said the inclusion of SAF in China’s 15th Five-Year Plan indicated that domestic blending requirements could be introduced in the coming years, although specific targets have not yet been announced.

China’s 2026–2030 plan, approved in March, identifies SAF as a fuel for development but does not establish aviation blending targets.

Hong Kong has separately set a target for SAF to account for 1%–3% of fuel used by departing flights by 2030. The target forms part of the city’s first Five-Year Plan, published in September.

The plan also supports SAF production in Dongguan, Guangdong province, where EcoCeres intends to build a plant with an annual capacity of 450,000 tonnes. The facility is scheduled to begin operations by 2030 and is expected to supply airports in Hong Kong, Shenzhen and Guangzhou.

Tam said the project remained on schedule. The reported investment of HK$10 billion ($1.27 billion) covers a 10-year development programme, while the refinery itself would cost considerably less.

Meeting the upper end of Hong Kong’s SAF target would require nearly half of the proposed plant’s output, according to Tam. Any remaining production could be exported to Europe, where the European Union has mandated a 6% SAF blending share by 2030.

Waste-based feedstocks underpin production strategy

Tam said EcoCeres had an advantage over some competitors because it owns its entire production technology system and does not depend on external technology licensors or catalyst suppliers.

The company uses waste-based raw materials, including used cooking oil collected from around 500,000 restaurants across China. Tam said the supply chain can trace the oil back to individual restaurants, providing airlines with information about the origin of the feedstock.

The use of waste-based materials is a key selling point for the company as airlines seek ways to reduce emissions from aviation.

Tam declined to disclose EcoCeres’ production costs, Reuters stated.

title: Europe looks to local agricultural waste to reduce reliance on imported SAF feedstocks
description:
NorSAF and Nova Pangaea have agreed to cooperate in Latvia on producing feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from locally sourced agricultural and forestry residues.
The project is aimed at reducing Europe’s dependence on imported SAF feedstocks.
Around 85% of feedstocks used for SAF production in Europe are currently imported, with China accounting for about 61% of supplies.
Nova Pangaea’s technology converts waste biomass into ethanol and biochar, with the ethanol then suitable for SAF production through the alcohol-to-jet pathway.
According to IATA estimates cited by the companies, Europe has sufficient biomass waste resources to support SAF production in line with its long-term targets through 2050.
text:
NorSAF and Nova Pangaea have agreed to cooperate in Latvia on producing feedstock for sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from locally sourced agricultural and forestry residues. The project is aimed at reducing Europe’s dependence on imported SAF feedstocks.

Around 85% of feedstocks used for SAF production in Europe are currently imported, with China accounting for about 61% of supplies. A large share of European production capacity relies on HEFA technology, which requires significant volumes of feedstocks such as used cooking oil.

The Latvian project plans to use agricultural and forestry residues available in the region. Nova Pangaea’s technology converts waste biomass into ethanol and biochar, with the ethanol then suitable for SAF production through the alcohol-to-jet pathway.

Demand for SAF in the EU is set to increase rapidly under ReFuelEU Aviation requirements. The share of SAF in fuel supplied at EU airports is set to rise from 2% in 2025 to 6% in 2030 and 20% in 2035, increasing the need for a stable and diversified feedstock base.

NorSAF expects the use of local waste resources to create a more resilient SAF supply chain in the Baltic region and reduce dependence on imported used cooking oil. According to IATA estimates cited by the companies, Europe has sufficient biomass waste resources to support SAF production in line with its long-term targets through 2050.

title: Can green jet fuel take off fast enough? - Swissinfo.ch
authors: Simon Bradley, Kai Reusser, this author English Department, this author Multimedia
description:
The pilot plant converts renewable methanol, made from green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide (CO₂), into synthetic jet fuel.
Until recently, synthetic jet fuel was largely confined to laboratories.
A catalytic process then converts the methanol into synthetic kerosene chemically identical to conventional jet fuel.
Sustainable jet fuel presently costs two to six times more than fossil keroseneExternal link, depending on the production pathway.
Read more: The Swiss firm that wants to power planes with green jet fuel
text:
A Swiss start-up aims to produce clean jet fuel from renewable methanol. But while the promising technology is attracting airlines, investors and policymakers, a critical challenge remains: can sustainable aviation fuels be scaled fast and cheap enough to decarbonise global air travel?

In late August the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) and Swiss start-up Metafuels inaugurated the world’s first methanol-to-jet fuel demonstration plant at the institute’s campus in Villigen, canton Aargau.

“Sustainable aviation fuel is the single most important lever we have to decarbonise aviation,” declared Metafuels CEO Saurabh Kapoor at the inauguration event.

The pilot plant converts renewable methanol, made from green hydrogen and captured carbon dioxide (CO₂), into synthetic jet fuel. Recently certified for aviation use, it can cut lifecycle emissions – across manufacturing, transport and flight operations – by up to 90% compared with fossil kerosene and can be used in existing aircraft.

Until recently, synthetic jet fuel was largely confined to laboratories. Today, certified fuels are entering commercial aviation, meaning the industry’s biggest challenge is no longer proving the technology works but whether it can be produced at sufficient scale in time and at an affordable cost.

Why the Swiss approach is different

Aviation accounts for roughly 2-3% of global CO₂ emissionsExternal link and is among the fastest-growing sources of greenhouse gases. Because long-haul flights cannot yet be electrified, sustainable aviation fuels (SAF) – and ultimately synthetic e-fuels like the one by Metafuels – are widely seen by the aviation industry as the main decarbonisation pathway, potentially delivering up to 65% of emissions reductions by 2050.External link

According to the World Economic Forum,External link the US leads commercial deployment, China is rapidly expanding capacity and Europe is at the forefront of policy-driven innovation in advanced fuels.

SAF can be produced from various sources. More than 80% of SAF currently comes from waste oils and fats, but limited supplies have shifted attention to e-SAF made from renewable electricity, hydrogen, and captured CO₂.

Metafuels combines green hydrogen, generated via water electrolysis using renewable power, with captured CO₂ from biogenic sources (plants, wood or waste) or direct air capture to create green methanol. A catalytic process then converts the methanol into synthetic kerosene chemically identical to conventional jet fuel.

Camille Mutrelle, a clean aviation expert at the Brussels-based NGO Transport & Environment,External link says methanol-to-jet fuels stand out because they can be made using renewable hydrogen and captured CO₂, rather than sources with limited availability like waste oils or agricultural crops, making larger-scale production possible.

“Methanol-to-jet is not a silver bullet,” Mutrelle told Swissinfo, but she sees it as one of the most promising e-fuel technologies for helping the aviation sector cut emissions over the long term.

Can production keep up?

Metafuels is developing its first industrial-scale plant in the Dutch port of Rotterdam, aiming to produce 10 tonnes of fuel per day by 2028 and 1,000 tonnes per day by the mid-2030s.

Achieving net-zero aviation by 2050 is expected to require around 500 million tonnes of SAF annually.External link Without stronger incentives, supply is unlikely to match the industry’s climate goals, says the International Air Transport Association (IATA).

Global output will reach just 2.4 million tonnes in 2026. Production volumes are “disappointing”, far below what will be needed to decarbonise air travel, IATA Director General Willie Walsh saidExternal link in June. He blamed weak government policies and insufficient investment from major oil firms.

Experts also warn that many announced projects never reach production.

“Of the SAF production capacity announced as expected to be operational by the end of 2026, our recent analysisExternal link found that only 24% had been completed, while 26% had been paused or cancelled,” Alessandro Martulli, environmental economics researcher at Hasselt University, told Swissinfo. He said project announcements are an unreliable guide to future supply because many never proceed to construction.

Whether Metafuels succeeds depends on overcoming the wider industry challenges: high production costs, financing and access to renewable energy and feedstocks.

Multiple obstacles

Scaling SAF remains constrained by cost, energy and resource requirements. Sustainable jet fuel presently costs two to six times more than fossil keroseneExternal link, depending on the production pathway.

Producing synthetic fuels requires vast amounts of renewable electricity, green hydrogen, water and CO2. A 2025 report by consultancy EYExternal link estimates that between $1 trillion to $1.5 trillion must be invested in SAF production by 2050 to reach net zero.

Mutrelle argues the biggest bottleneck is not technology but a lack of commitment from major fuel suppliers.

“The oil and gas sector clearly possesses the necessary capital. Europe has over 40 planned industrial e-SAF projectsExternal link, yet not a single one has reached a Final Investment Decision,” she said. Fuel suppliers who have to meet quotas under Europe’s ReFuelEUExternal link regulation have been slow to commit to the long-term purchase agreements needed to unlock investment, she added.

Martulli points to rising project costs, limited competitiveness of SAF, and shortages of key inputs such as affordable green hydrogen and biogenic CO₂.

Is regulation ahead of reality?

More than 100 airlines have started using SAFs. Swiss International Air Lines (SWISS) currently uses it for 0.9% of its fuel consumption, all of it produced from biogenic residues such as used cooking oilsExternal link. To secure future supplies, it has partnered with Metafuels and another e-SAF producer, ETH Zurich spinoff Synhelion.

“As a customer we are basically ready and could be transformed tomorrow if there was enough sustainable fuel available at the right price,” Jens Fehlinger, CEO of SWISS, told attendees at the recent Metafuels/PSI inauguration event.

Under EU rules, airlines must gradually increase SAF use, reaching 70% by 2050. Switzerland has aligned its revised CO₂ Act with the same targets.

Some industry observers fear regulators are mandating aviation decarbonisation faster than production can keep up, risking higher fares.

“The 2030 e-SAF targets by the UK and the EU are beyond unrealistic,” says Marie Owens Thomsen, IATA’s Senior Vice President Sustainability and Chief Economist. IATA notes that the EU and the UK will require about 0.6 million tonnes of e-SAF by 2030, while current operating and under-construction capacity amounts to only 0.02 million tonnes.

“For the non-e-SAF component of the European mandate, announced capacity could, in principle, be sufficient by 2030,” said Martulli. But e-SAF remains a major concern, with only a small fraction of proposed EU production projects progressing to a final investment decision, threatening future supply targets.

Despite these concerns, the researcher says the targets remain achievable if governments reduce investment risks and provide long-term support and certainty, as they did for wind and solar power.

IATA saysExternal link accelerating SAF adoption will require coordinated action to expand renewable energy and supply of fuel sources, ensure open access to fuel infrastructure and strengthen policy and investment frameworks, as well as creating a global SAF market.

Yet e-SAF remains scarce, and some experts argue technology alone cannot offset continued growth in air travel.

“Our studies at [the Paul Scherrer Institute] have shown that SAF will not be enough. We also have to reduce the number of flights,” said Marco Ranocchiari, head of energy system integration at the institute.

As companies such as Metafuels race to scale synthetic fuel production, the next few years will test whether policy, technology and investment can bridge the gap between climate ambitions and the realities of aviation growth.

Edited by Gabe Bullard/Veronica De Vore

title: Singapore's $118m push to grow bioeconomy sector | The Straits Times

SINGAPORE - Singapore wants to harness nature’s living “factories” to produce enzymes, chemicals and materials – some of which can replace fossil fuels – with a $118 million push to grow its bioeconomy sector.
The Bioeconomy Funding Initiative was announced on Oct 5 by Education Minister Desmond Lee at the launch of the National Centre for Engineering Biology.
The effort is Singapore’s largest funding tranche for developing the bioeconomy sector, according to the government agencies.

text:
SINGAPORE - Singapore wants to harness nature’s living “factories” to produce enzymes, chemicals and materials – some of which can replace fossil fuels – with a $118 million push to grow its bioeconomy sector.

Such products include sustainable aviation fuel, which can replace petroleum-based jet fuel. Polymers made from castor oil can be substituted for plastics made from crude oil, while using biomethane for energy can reduce the need to burn fossil-based natural gas.

The Bioeconomy Funding Initiative was announced on Oct 5 by Education Minister Desmond Lee at the launch of the National Centre for Engineering Biology.

The Economic Development Board (EDB) and A*STAR are driving the effort . Its launch comes amid projections that the global market for such materials and chemicals could exceed US$200 billion (S$256 billion) by 2030.

The effort is Singapore’s largest funding tranche for developing the bioeconomy sector, according to the government agencies.

The initiative joins existing funding of about $82 million and contributes to a total commitment of some $ 200 million for bioeconomy-related projects over the next five years.

EDB’s managing director Jermaine Loy said at the launch event at the National University of Singapore (NUS) that the promising outlook for the bioeconomy is driven in part by the roll-out of regulations spurring firms to look for alternatives to raw materials dependent on fossil fuels.

Biological sciences are increasingly used to make products that outperform existing ones in areas such as agricultural crop protection and consumer care, he added.

Against this backdrop, the fund will build research capabilities in areas where Singapore has an advantage to tackle challenges flagged by local companies, start-ups and investors, including its position in South-east Asia, where most of the world’s palm oil is produced.

“Our ambition is for the bioeconomy to become a new source of growth for Singapore,” said Loy.

He said the bioeconomy could create new business opportunities in the development of speciality chemicals and advanced materials, good jobs and new career pathways for Singaporeans.

EDB said this emerging area could also strengthen Singapore’s energy and chemical sector, which today accounts for about 20% of the country’s total manufacturing output.

EDB vice-president for chemicals and materials Kelly Lai said Singapore’s strong energy and chemicals sector, as well as expertise in synthetic biology and research and innovation, will enable the country to better tap opportunities in the bioeconomy.

Lai said: “Home to a diverse range of companies – from global majors to specialised players – with a long-term presence here to serve demand across Asia, (the sector) has the depth and scale to pursue new growth pathways.

“The bioeconomy gives these companies new tools to diversify raw material sources, develop novel high-value products and produce more sustainable chemicals and materials, supporting Singapore’s broader push into speciality chemicals and advanced materials.”

For instance, researchers at the HH@NUS SINERGY Laboratory – a partnership between NUS and industrial polymer firm Huahao Chemical – have found a way to use living cells as factories to make building blocks for a polymer in fibres and fabrics .

The initiative will focus on four areas.

The first aims to transform underused agricultural waste from the production of biodegradable fuels – such as crude glycerol from palm residue – into cheaper , sustainable r aw materials.

The second seeks to engineer microbes and enzyme s using advanced tools, including artificial intelligence.

The third looks at improving industrial-scale processes using smart monitoring and digital technologies to reduce waste and lower costs.

The final area will identify the most effective ways to produce commercially relevant products such as high-grade synthetic rubbers and cosmetic ingredients.

Projects under the initiative will be managed by the new Bioeconomy Innovation Office in A* STAR , which will help promising innovations reach adoption and commercialisation.

A*STAR’s interim programme director for the Bioeconomy Innovation Office Wong Min Hao said the fund will help boost the resilience of supply chains by finding materials to reduce reliance on petrochemicals.

He cited the region’s unique waste streams of palm oil, cassava, tapioca and rice as areas Singapore could look into. If successful, this could mean using dyes made of such materials instead of petrochemicals, he added.

Ultimately, the fund aims to push for more commercial outcomes at the end of five years, said Wong.

New centre for engineering biology

Meanwhile, the National Centre for Engineering Biology – hosted at NUS – will nurture scientists and innovators who will shape the field that programmes and harnesses living cells, said Lee.

He was speaking at the opening of the inaugural Singapore Engineering Biology Week, which brings together those in the field.

He added: “Students and researchers will work across disciplines and institutions, and engage industry on real-world needs.

“In doing so, they will deepen their expertise and make an impact.”

Officially opened on Oct 5, the centre is supported by a National Research Foundation grant of nearly $50 million, awarded over seven years starting in 2023.

It brings together Singapore’s institutes of higher learning, including NUS, Nanyang Technological University and the Singapore Institute of Technology.

The centre will focus on building knowledge and technologies in engineering biology for the sustainable biomanufacturing of speciality chemicals, such as flavour and fragrance compounds.

Its ongoing flagship project, led by NUS, focuses on AI-guided engineering biology for sustainable speciality chemicals. It aims to engineer microbes and enzymes that can convert renewable feedstocks – organic materials used to create fuels and other chemicals – into speciality chemicals.

Said the centre’s executive director Matthew Chang: “Our goal is to enable more sustainable ways of making products that society depends on, using renewable feedstocks and cleaner manufacturing processes.”

More than 150 researchers , students and professional staff contribute to the centre’s work across partner institutions.

Recruitment is ongoing for about 50 more roles, the centre’s institutes of higher learning said in a statement.

These positions include principal investigators, postdoctoral researchers and graduate students, as well as technical, engineering, laboratory support and centre management staff.

title: Ethereum Goes Private for AI, Dogecoin Adds DeFi, and Blast Calls It Quits - YouHodler
description:
Ethereum Takes Privacy Into AI Payments The Ethereum Foundation and Open Anonymity Project launched zkAPI on Ethereum mainnet, allowing users to pay for access to AI models without directly linking their identity to the questions they submit.
Dogecoin Gets a Smart-Contract Layer DogeOS launched a public testnet for an EVM-compatible zero-knowledge rollup that settles to Dogecoin.
The system is intended to support DeFi, stablecoins, prediction markets and games without requiring major changes to the Dogecoin base layer.
The more interesting part is not simply that another blockchain security concern appeared.
As AI improves, projects may have to become better at slowing things down when necessary without making normal development unnecessarily difficult.
text:
Highlights

Ethereum Foundation and Open Anonymity Project launched zkAPI for private AI payments

DogeOS opened a public testnet bringing smart contracts to Dogecoin

Petrobras is testing Cardano for sustainable fuel and emissions tracking

Aztec Labs relaunched zk.money as a private wallet on its Ethereum Layer 2

Blast will shut down after network operating costs exceeded revenue

Polymarket and Kalshi are expanding further into equity-linked prediction markets

NEAR Intents halted services after an exploit estimated at about $3.8 million

Arbitrum paused new Stylus activations over risks linked to AI-assisted attacks

Crypto infrastructure is finding its way into more practical parts of the digital economy. Privacy tools are being applied to AI payments, established networks are gaining new functionality, and blockchain systems are being tested in areas ranging from industrial tracking to event-driven financial markets.

‍

At the same time, the operational side remains difficult. Network economics, cross-chain security and new attack methods continue to test whether promising technology can turn into products that are secure, useful and financially sustainable.

Ethereum Takes Privacy Into AI Payments

The Ethereum Foundation and Open Anonymity Project launched zkAPI on Ethereum mainnet, allowing users to pay for access to AI models without directly linking their identity to the questions they submit. Users prepay in USDC, while zero-knowledge proofs confirm access without exposing the same payment information each time a request is made.

‍

The idea addresses a fairly straightforward problem. Paying for an online service usually creates a connection between the user, the payment method and the activity taking place on the account. With AI, that link can be more sensitive because prompts may contain information about work, finances, research or other subjects a user may not want permanently attached to their identity.

‍

What makes zkAPI interesting is that crypto is not the end product here. Blockchain is being used as an underlying payment and privacy layer for a service that already exists outside the industry, which is a more practical role than creating another standalone financial product.

‍

The challenge will be usability. Privacy technology has often struggled when users are expected to understand unfamiliar tools or complex mechanics, so the real test is whether systems such as zkAPI can make the privacy element almost invisible while still doing the job in the background.

Dogecoin Gets a Smart-Contract Layer

DogeOS launched a public testnet for an EVM-compatible zero-knowledge rollup that settles to Dogecoin. The system is intended to support DeFi, stablecoins, prediction markets and games without requiring major changes to the Dogecoin base layer.

‍

That gives DOGE a path into areas where it has historically had little presence. Dogecoin has largely remained a simple transfer network with a large community and a recognisable asset, rather than a platform built around programmable applications. EVM compatibility could make DogeOS more familiar to developers who already work with Ethereum-style smart contracts.

The harder part starts after the testnet. Crypto already has plenty of networks capable of supporting DeFi, games and stablecoins, so DogeOS will need applications people actually want to use, enough liquidity to support them and a reason for DOGE holders to move beyond basic transfers.

Petrobras Tests Cardano in Fuel Tracking

Brazilian state oil giant Petrobras is testing Cardano in two research projects involving sustainable aviation fuel and renewable diesel. The blockchain would be used to create traceable records and reduce the risk that the same emissions reduction is counted more than once.

‍

This is a very different use of blockchain from most products that attract attention in crypto markets. There is no obvious speculative element and no need to build a token economy around the data. The value, if the system works, would come from giving several parties a consistent record they can verify.

‍

That can matter in supply chains where multiple companies handle the same product or rely on the same environmental information. Once sustainability claims have reporting or financial consequences, disagreements over who recorded what and when can become expensive. A shared ledger could reduce some of that friction, particularly if it makes duplication easier to detect.

But Cardano still has to prove that blockchain adds something conventional databases cannot provide efficiently enough. For enterprise applications like this, the technology is most convincing when it quietly improves coordination and auditability rather than becoming the centre of the story.

Aztec Brings zk.money Back

Aztec Labs has relaunched zk.money three years after shutting down the original service, this time running it on the Aztec Ethereum Layer 2. The wallet is designed to keep balances, payment amounts and counterparties private, while users can receive funds through readable handles such as bob.zk.money.

‍

The combination matters because privacy has often come with a usability cost. Users may understand why they want less financial information exposed, but they are less likely to use a product regularly if sending money requires extra steps, unfamiliar addresses or specialist knowledge. Human-readable handles do not solve every usability problem, but they make the experience feel closer to an ordinary payments product.

‍

There is still a difficult balance to manage. Private transactions are attractive precisely because less information is visible, while financial infrastructure also has to deal with operational controls and accountability. For zk.money, the challenge is therefore not only to make privacy technically strong, but to make it practical enough for ordinary use.

Blast Runs Out of Economic Room

Paradigm-backed Blast announced that it will wind down after concluding that the cost of operating the network exceeds the revenue it generates. The Layer 2 once held more than $2 billion in total value locked, but that figure later fell to roughly $32 million.

‍

The contrast is striking because Blast had already demonstrated that it could attract capital. What it did not prove was that those deposits could translate into durable economic activity once the early attention faded. Development, infrastructure and maintenance still have to be paid for even when liquidity moves elsewhere.

‍

That makes the story relevant beyond Blast itself. Crypto often treats TVL and deposit growth as shorthand for success, but those numbers can be misleading when incentives or short-term demand play a large role. A network can look healthy while money is arriving and still struggle to support itself once those flows reverse.

‍

For smaller Layer 2 networks, this is an uncomfortable reality. Users can move capital quickly and developers have many competing ecosystems to choose from, so retaining activity can be much harder than attracting it. Blast reached scale, but scale alone was not enough to keep the economics working.

Prediction Markets Move Closer to Stocks

Polymarket and Kalshi are moving further into equity-linked prediction markets, with contracts connected to companies such as Tesla, Apple and Nvidia. More than $220 million had already been traded in equity-linked markets on Polymarket, showing that the format is drawing meaningful interest.

‍

The attraction is easy to understand. A prediction market reduces a complex view to a defined outcome, allowing users to express an opinion without building a conventional position through shares, options or another financial instrument. That simplicity is part of what makes the format accessible.

‍

Once those contracts are tied directly to listed companies, however, the line between a prediction market and traditional financial exposure becomes less clear. The structure is different, but the economic motivation can be very similar if users are effectively taking views on earnings, corporate events or other stock-related outcomes. That puts more pressure on liquidity, settlement rules and contract wording as the products move closer to mainstream financial markets.

NEAR Intents Faces a $3.8 Million Exploit

NEAR Intents temporarily halted services after an exploit estimated at around $3.8 million. The project said affected users would be fully compensated, reducing the immediate financial damage for users but leaving the underlying security problem to be addressed.

‍

The incident reflects the trade-off built into cross-chain infrastructure. These systems are designed to make moving value between networks easier, but that convenience depends on several components working correctly together. Every additional layer or connection introduces another place where something can fail.

‍

Compensation matters, but reimbursement is still a response rather than a security control. The more important questions concern how quickly the issue was identified, how effectively it was contained and what changes are made before normal activity resumes.

Arbitrum Confronts AI-Assisted Security Risk

Arbitrum temporarily paused new Stylus activations after researchers identified risks involving AI-assisted attacks. Existing programs continued operating while new activations were stopped as the issue was assessed.

The more interesting part is not simply that another blockchain security concern appeared. AI is beginning to influence both sides of the security process, helping developers review code while also giving attackers faster ways to search for weaknesses.

‍

That changes the operating assumptions for blockchain infrastructure. If vulnerabilities can be found faster, projects may have less time between introducing a flaw and seeing someone attempt to exploit it. Deployment controls, testing procedures and emergency responses therefore become more important alongside the code itself.

Arbitrum's response captures that tension well. Open networks are designed to let developers build and deploy quickly, while security sometimes requires exactly the opposite. As AI improves, projects may have to become better at slowing things down when necessary without making normal development unnecessarily difficult.

Bottom Line

The stronger stories point toward crypto infrastructure being used in narrower and more practical ways. Privacy is being applied to AI access and payments, Dogecoin is gaining a route into programmable applications, blockchain is being tested for industrial record keeping, and prediction markets are moving closer to traditional financial activity. These developments are easier to judge because their value depends on whether the product solves a real problem rather than on whether a token attracts attention.

‍

The weaknesses are just as visible. Blast shows that liquidity can disappear long before network costs do, NEAR Intents shows how cross-chain convenience can increase operational exposure, and Arbitrum shows how AI may raise the speed and complexity of security threats. The projects that hold up over time will need more than interesting technology. They will need sound economics, clear market design and systems that can keep working when something goes wrong.

text:
A bipartisan proposal in the US Senate seeks to extend a tax credit for small biodiesel producers through 2029, continuing support for companies that use domestically sourced agricultural feedstocks, JC Post reported.

Republican Senator Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Democratic Senator Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota have introduced legislation to extend the Small Agri-Biodiesel Producer Credit, which is scheduled to expire on December 31.

Under the credit, eligible biodiesel producers receive 20 cents per gallon on the first 15 million gallons of biodiesel produced each year. To qualify, companies must have annual production capacity of no more than 60 million gallons and use domestic agricultural feedstocks.

The proposed legislation would extend the credit for three additional years. Without congressional action, the incentive will expire at the end of 2026.

Clean Fuels Alliance America has backed the proposed extension. The organisation said small biodiesel producers contribute to rural employment and domestic energy production while supplying renewable fuel at lower cost.

The proposed extension would maintain the tax incentive for small producers through 2029.

title: IndiGo revises fuel charges as ATF prices surge
description:
IndiGo will revise fuel charges across its domestic and international routes from October 6, citing a sustained increase in Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) costs.
The revised charges will apply to all new bookings made after 0001 hours on October 6, 2026.
IndiGo said ATF prices have remained volatile in recent months, with geopolitical developments in the Middle East contributing to the increase.
The charge will be INR 6,000 for flights to Africa and INR 10,000 for flights to Europe.
IndiGo said the revised charges represent a relatively modest adjustment compared with the increase that would have been required to fully offset higher fuel costs.
text: IndiGo will revise fuel charges across its domestic and international routes from October 6, citing a sustained increase in Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) costs. The revised charges will apply to all new bookings made after 0001 hours on October 6, 2026. IndiGo said ATF prices have remained volatile in recent months, with geopolitical developments in the Middle East contributing to the increase. The airline said the latest month-on-month rise in fuel prices has exceeded 14%, taking ATF costs to among their highest levels in the past decade. Fuel represents a significant component of airline operating costs and the increase is expected to affect cost structures and network economics. Under the revised domestic fuel charge structure, passengers will pay INR 375 for routes up to 500 km, INR 600 for routes between 501 km and 1,000 km, INR 900 for routes between 1,001 km and 1,500 km, INR 1,150 for routes between 1,501 km and 2,000 km, and INR 1,300 for routes above 2,000 km. For international flights, the revised charge will be INR 1,000 for SAARC routes up to 500 km and INR 3,000 for SAARC routes of 501 km and above. Flights to Southeast Asia, the GCC and Middle East, and North and East Asia will attract a fuel charge of INR 5,500. The charge will be INR 6,000 for flights to Africa and INR 10,000 for flights to Europe. IndiGo said the revised charges represent a relatively modest adjustment compared with the increase that would have been required to fully offset higher fuel costs. The airline said it would continue to monitor fuel prices and the broader operating environment and make further adjustments when required. IndiGo added that the revised charges would result in an additional cost for customers but said the adjustment was necessary in view of sustained increases in operating costs.

title: EU SAF supply exceeds first ReFuelEU target - Oils & Fats International
description:
The volume of SAF accounted for 2.79% of total aviation fuel supplied by EU airline operators, the report said.
A further 120,000 tonnes – around 11% – was classified as other aviation biofuels, while 90,000 tonnes – about 8% - was advanced aviation biofuels.
According to EASA data, the Netherlands was the largest destination for SAF supplied in the EU, receiving 320,000 tonnes – 29% of total reported SAF.

text:
The volume of SAF accounted for 2.79% of total aviation fuel supplied by EU airline operators, the report said.

Alongside the increase, there was a wider expansion in physical SAF availability, which was supplied at 121 EU airports across all 27 EU member states in 2025, equivalent to 79% of EU airports.

However, the market remained heavily reliant on imported feedstocks and conventional hydrotreated esters and fatty acids (HEFA)-based pathways, the 28 September report said.

The ReFuelEU aviation targets calls for a minimum 2% SAF share in aviation fuel supplied at EU airports in 2025, rising to 6% in 2030, and 70% in 2050.

Of the 1.1M tonnes supplied in 2025, 885,000 tonnes – around 80% of the total volume – was classified as aviation fuel produced from feedstocks listed under Annex IX Part B of the EU Renewable Energy Directive.

A further 120,000 tonnes – around 11% – was classified as other aviation biofuels, while 90,000 tonnes – about 8% - was advanced aviation biofuels.

Used cooking oil (UCO) accounted for 80% of the total SAF feedstock mix, broadly unchanged from 81% in 2024.

The remaining 20% included category 3 animal fats at 11%, palm oil mill effluent (POME) at 5%, with food waste, crude tall oil (CTO) and category 1 and 2 animal fats making up the balance.

Synthetic aviation fuel did not contribute to aircraft operators’ reported SAF purchases in 2025, while 69.6% of the 1M tonnes purchased by aircraft operators was classified as aviation biofuel.

Imported feedstocks continued to dominate the supply chain, with EASA finding that 85% of feedstock used to produce the SAF originated outside the EU.

China accounted for 61% of feedstock origin, followed by Malaysia at 8%, Indonesia at 5% and the UK at 3%. Only 15% of feedstock originated within the EU.

“The 2025 data shows a European SAF supply chain that is increasingly capable of processing and supplying SAF domestically but remains highly exposed to international feedstock flows,” Fastmarkets wrote.

“This is particularly relevant for the HEFA market, where UCO, animal fats and other waste-based feedstocks compete across renewable diesel, SAF and other renewable fuel applications.”

The data also showed that not all the 1.1M tonnes reported by suppliers was intended to count towards the ReFuelEU minimum share, with around 250,000 tonnes reported as voluntary SAF. That volume represented almost one-quarter of total reported SAF supply.

Meanwhile, EASA added that 1.1M tonnes could be a slight underestimate of actual EU SAF supply as around 10% of obligated fuel suppliers had not reported SAF volumes and the reporting system did not capture SAF supplied to non-EU airports.

According to EASA data, the Netherlands was the largest destination for SAF supplied in the EU, receiving 320,000 tonnes – 29% of total reported SAF.

Spain received 152,000 tonnes, Germany 116,000 tonnes, Italy 111,000 tonnes and France 107,000 tonnes. Together, those five countries accounted for about 74% of EU SAF supply.

At airport level, Amsterdam Schiphol accounted for 29% of total SAF supplied, followed by Frankfurt at 8% and Paris Charles de Gaulle at 7%.

According to EASA’s 2030 capacity assessment, although proposed EU production capacity was sufficient, project execution was important.

The agency estimated that current operational facilities would provide around 1.5M tonnes/year of SAF capacity by 2030, below the approximately 2.1M tonnes required to meet the 6% ReFuelEU SAF minimum share, excluding synthetic aviation fuels.

When facilities under construction or that had reached final investment decision (FID) were included, potential capacity increased to 3.7M tonnes/year.

A wider scenario that included projects classified as having a high level of credibility put potential SAF capacity at 5.5M tonnes/year, plus 600,000 tonnes/year of eSAF capacity.

According to demand-side data, aircraft operators reported purchasing around 1M tonnes of SAF in 2025, with 245 operators reporting SAF purchases.

The top 10 operators accounted for approximately half of those purchases, with KLM reporting the largest volume at 91,786 tonnes, followed by Ryanair at 78,951 tonnes and Transavia at 68,003 tonnes.

Of the SAF purchased by operators, 624,000 tonnes was reported as intended to be claimed under market-based measures. Of that amount, 512,000 tonnes, or 49% of total SAF purchased, was associated with the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS), 90,000 tonnes with the UK Emissions Trading Scheme (UK ETS) and the equivalent of 2% with the Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA).

Another 415,000 tonnes, or 40% of eligible fuel, was not claimed under a market-based measure.

EASA also published 2025 reference prices, with aviation biofuels at €1,925 (US$2,174)/tonne compared with €640 (US$723)/tonne for conventional aviation fuel, implying a reference-price gap of about €1,285 (US$1,452)/tonne, with aviation biofuels priced at around three times the conventional fuel reference price.

title: IndiGo Hikes Fuel Surcharge on Flights Amid Rising Jet Fuel Prices - Rediff Money
description: IndiGo announces a hike in fuel surcharge for domestic and international flights starting Oct 6 due to rising jet fuel prices, leading to higher airfares.
text: Key PointsIndiGo will increase fuel surcharges for domestic and international flights effective October 6.The hike is a direct response to the continuous rise in jet fuel (ATF) prices, which are at a decade-high.Domestic flight surcharges will range from Rs 100 to Rs 350, with specific amounts for different distances and international routes.This marks IndiGos second fuel surcharge increase since April, impacting overall airfares.The airline stated it made a modest adjustment to minimize customer impact despite significant operating cost increases.New Delhi, Oct 5 (PTI) The countrys largest airline IndiGo on Monday announced a hike in fuel surcharge for domestic and international flights in the wake of rising jet fuel prices. The revised charges will be effective from October 6, and the move will push airfares higher. The quantum of the hike ranges from Rs 100 to Rs 350 for domestic flights depending on distance. The hike in surcharge has also been effected for international flights. This is the second time since April that the carrier has increased the fuel surcharge, which was introduced in March. The fuel surcharge will be Rs 375 for routes with distance up to 500 kilometres and Rs 600 for flights having distance between 501 to 1,000 kilometres. The amount will be Rs 900 for routes with distance of 1,001 to 1,500 kilometres and Rs 1,150 for a distance of 1,501 to 2,000 kilometres. The statement said the fuel surcharge will be Rs 1,300 for flights having a distance of more than 2,000 kilometres. For the SAARC region flights, the fuel surcharge varies from Rs 1,000 to Rs 3,000 and Rs 6,000 for Africa flights and Rs 10,000 for Europe services. The fuel surcharge will be Rs 5,500 for flights to Southeast Asia, GCC and the Middle East, and North and East Asia, as per the statement. IndiGo said ATF prices have remained volatile in recent months, especially following the geopolitical situation in the Middle East. According to the airline, the continuous rise in fuel prices, with the latest month-on-month increase exceeding 14 per cent, has taken ATF costs to levels that are amongst the highest in the last decade. Given that Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) makes up a significant share of the airlines operating costs, this rise is expected to impact airlines cost structures and network economics, including those of IndiGo, it said in a statement on Monday. In view of the situation, the airline said it has marginally re-calibrated its fuel charges across its domestic as well as international flights. While offsetting the increase in fuel costs would have required a significantly larger increase in the fuel charges, a measured and relatively modest adjustment to minimise the impact on customers has been made, the airline said. Regretting the additional burden the revised fuel charges would have on the travellers, the airline said the decision reflects the sustained increase in operating costs and the evolving market environment. The airline also said it would continue to monitor the situation and make relevant adjustments as and when appropriate. IndiGo operates over 2,200 flights daily.

title: BookBetter: Νέα πλατφόρμα συγκρίνει πτήσεις με βάση τιμή και κλιματικό αποτύπωμα
description:
Μια νέα πλατφόρμα κρατήσεων αεροπορικών εισιτηρίων επιχειρεί να ενσωματώσει το κλιματικό αποτύπωμα απευθείας στη διαδικασία επιλογής πτήσης, επιτρέποντας παράλληλα στους ταξιδιώτες να συνεισφέρουν στην αγορά Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).
Η προσέγγιση έρχεται σε μια περίοδο κατά την οποία η αεροπορία βρίσκεται υπό αυξανόμενη πίεση να περιορίσει το κλιματικό της αποτύπωμα.
Η BookBetter επιχειρεί να διαφοροποιηθεί από άλλες υπηρεσίες αναζήτησης πτήσεων μέσω της δυνατότητας αγοράς συνεισφοράς σε Sustainable Aviation Fuel.
Η διαφορά, σύμφωνα με το δημοσίευμα, είναι ότι η BookBetter επιτρέπει στον χρήστη να αγοράσει άμεσα συνεισφορά για SAF.
Ο αλγόριθμος της πλατφόρμας συνδυάζει κόστος και περιβαλλοντικό αποτύπωμα, ώστε οι επιλογές με χαμηλότερες εκπομπές να μην ταυτίζονται αναγκαστικά με τις ακριβότερες πτήσεις.
text:
Μια νέα πλατφόρμα κρατήσεων αεροπορικών εισιτηρίων επιχειρεί να ενσωματώσει το κλιματικό αποτύπωμα απευθείας στη διαδικασία επιλογής πτήσης, επιτρέποντας παράλληλα στους ταξιδιώτες να συνεισφέρουν στην αγορά Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

.

Η BookBetter κατατάσσει τις διαθέσιμες πτήσεις συνδυάζοντας την τιμή με τις εκπομπές ανά επιβάτη και τον πιθανό αντίκτυπο των contrails, των γραμμών συμπύκνωσης που σχηματίζονται σε μεγάλο ύψος και μπορούν να συμβάλουν στη θέρμανση της ατμόσφαιρας.

Σύμφωνα με το Travel + Leisure, η πλατφόρμα έχει σχεδιαστεί ώστε ο ταξιδιώτης να μπορεί να συγκρίνει διαφορετικές διαδρομές όχι μόνο ως προς το κόστος, αλλά και ως προς την περιβαλλοντική τους επίδοση, πριν ολοκληρώσει την κράτηση.

Η προσέγγιση έρχεται σε μια περίοδο κατά την οποία η αεροπορία βρίσκεται υπό αυξανόμενη πίεση να περιορίσει το κλιματικό της αποτύπωμα. Ένα υπερατλαντικό ταξίδι μετ’ επιστροφής μπορεί, ανάλογα με τη διαδρομή και τον τύπο αεροσκάφους, να δημιουργήσει ανά επιβάτη οικονομικής θέσης ποσότητα CO₂ συγκρίσιμη με τις εκπομπές ενός τυπικού αμερικανικού αυτοκινήτου για περίπου δύο μήνες.

Παράλληλα, το Travel + Leisure σημειώνει ότι η αεροπορία ευθύνεται για σχεδόν 4% της παρατηρούμενης ανθρωπογενούς υπερθέρμανσης μέχρι σήμερα, επικαλούμενο σχετική επιστημονική μελέτη.

Το περιβαλλοντικό ζήτημα δεν περιορίζεται στις υπερατλαντικές πτήσεις. Οι μικρές εσωτερικές διαδρομές μπορεί να εμφανίζουν υψηλές εκπομπές ανά μίλι, καθώς σημαντικό μέρος της κατανάλωσης καυσίμου πραγματοποιείται κατά την απογείωση και την άνοδο, προτού το αεροσκάφος φθάσει στο αποδοτικότερο ύψος πτήσης.

Η BookBetter επιχειρεί να διαφοροποιηθεί από άλλες υπηρεσίες αναζήτησης πτήσεων μέσω της δυνατότητας αγοράς συνεισφοράς σε Sustainable Aviation Fuel.

Το SAF αποτελεί εναλλακτική λύση έναντι του συμβατικού jet fuel και, ανάλογα με την πρώτη ύλη και τη μέθοδο παραγωγής του, μπορεί να μειώσει σημαντικά τις εκπομπές αερίων του θερμοκηπίου σε ολόκληρο τον κύκλο ζωής του καυσίμου.

Δεν πρόκειται, ωστόσο, για λύση μηδενικών εκπομπών. Η κλιματική του επίδοση διαφέρει ανάλογα με τον τρόπο παραγωγής, η διαθέσιμη ποσότητα παραμένει περιορισμένη και η αγορά SAF μέσω συστημάτων book-and-claim δεν σημαίνει ότι το συγκεκριμένο καύσιμο θα χρησιμοποιηθεί στο αεροσκάφος του επιβάτη.

Η λογική του μοντέλου είναι διαφορετική: η δημιουργία πρόσθετης ζήτησης μπορεί να συμβάλει στην αύξηση της παραγωγής και στη μελλοντική μείωση της εξάρτησης της αεροπορίας από το συμβατικό ορυκτό kerosene.

Οι πελάτες της BookBetter που επιλέγουν να συνεισφέρουν στην αγορά SAF λαμβάνουν πιστοποιητικό στο οποίο αναγράφονται, μεταξύ άλλων, ένας μοναδικός αριθμός αναφοράς, ο παραγωγός του καυσίμου, το αεροδρόμιο στο οποίο παραδόθηκε και η εκτιμώμενη ποσότητα εκπομπών που αποφεύχθηκε.

Ο συνιδρυτής της πλατφόρμας Louis Lammertyn εξήγησε στο Travel + Leisure ότι η BookBetter δημιουργήθηκε μετά από χρόνια ενασχόλησης με εναλλακτικά αεροπορικά καύσιμα και σιδηροδρομικές μεταφορές, με την ομάδα να διαπιστώνει ότι οι τεχνικές λύσεις υπήρχαν ήδη αλλά δεν είχαν ενσωματωθεί αποτελεσματικά στην εμπειρία του ταξιδιώτη.

«Τα εργαλεία για να πετάμε καλύτερα υπάρχουν ήδη σήμερα. Απλώς δεν ήταν συνδεδεμένα με τον ταξιδιώτη που μπορούσε πραγματικά να τα χρησιμοποιήσει», ανέφερε.

Η πλατφόρμα επέλεξε συνειδητά να δίνει έμφαση στο SAF αντί στα παραδοσιακά carbon credits. Ο Lammertyn υποστήριξε ότι η επένδυση απευθείας στο καύσιμο συμβάλλει περισσότερο στον μετασχηματισμό του ίδιου του αεροπορικού κλάδου, αντί να χρηματοδοτεί ένα εξωτερικό έργο αντιστάθμισης ενώ οι αεροπορικές εκπομπές συνεχίζονται.

Η BookBetter δεν είναι η πρώτη υπηρεσία που παρουσιάζει δεδομένα εκπομπών κατά την αναζήτηση πτήσεων. Το Google Flights εμφανίζει εκτιμήσεις άνθρακα δίπλα στις τιμές από το 2021 και διαθέτει φίλτρο για πτήσεις χαμηλότερων εκπομπών, ενώ αντίστοιχα εργαλεία προσφέρει και η Skyscanner.

Η διαφορά, σύμφωνα με το δημοσίευμα, είναι ότι η BookBetter επιτρέπει στον χρήστη να αγοράσει άμεσα συνεισφορά για SAF.

Η τιμή παραμένει πάντως βασικό μέρος του μοντέλου. Ο αλγόριθμος της πλατφόρμας συνδυάζει κόστος και περιβαλλοντικό αποτύπωμα, ώστε οι επιλογές με χαμηλότερες εκπομπές να μην ταυτίζονται αναγκαστικά με τις ακριβότερες πτήσεις.

Στην πράξη, μια απευθείας πτήση με νεότερο αεροσκάφος και σε οικονομική θέση μπορεί να εμφανίζεται υψηλότερα στην κατάταξη τόσο επειδή είναι οικονομικότερη όσο και επειδή έχει μικρότερο αποτύπωμα από μια διαδρομή με ανταπόκριση ή μια θέση business class.

Ο Lammertyn αποφεύγει, πάντως, να χαρακτηρίσει τις αεροπορικές μετακινήσεις «πλήρως βιώσιμες». Όπως σημειώνει, ακόμη και με χρήση 100% SAF, μια πτήση εξακολουθεί να έχει αρνητικό κλιματικό αντίκτυπο, μεταξύ άλλων εξαιτίας των μη-CO₂ επιδράσεων της αεροπορίας.

Για τον ίδιο, η πλέον βιώσιμη επιλογή παραμένει το τρένο όπου αυτό είναι πρακτικά εφικτό. Για τον λόγο αυτό η BookBetter διαθέτει και ξεχωριστή επιλογή αναζήτησης σιδηροδρομικών ταξιδιών.

Περισσότεροι από 30.000 άνθρωποι έχουν ήδη δοκιμάσει την πλατφόρμα, σύμφωνα με τον συνιδρυτή της, μεταξύ των οποίων και ταξιδιώτες που δεν θεωρούν τη βιωσιμότητα βασικό κριτήριο στις αγορές τους.

Η περίπτωση της BookBetter δείχνει μια ευρύτερη μετατόπιση στον τουριστικό και αεροπορικό κλάδο: η περιβαλλοντική πληροφορία περνά σταδιακά από τις εταιρικές εκθέσεις βιωσιμότητας στο ίδιο το σημείο όπου ο καταναλωτής αποφασίζει τι θα αγοράσει.

title: The future of aviation starts on the ground: How is Menzies changing airport operations?
description:
Electric equipment also means less noise, better working conditions for employees, a more pleasant environment for passengers and more efficient daily operations.
We are particularly pleased that the first flights in the region to be fully serviced with electric ground equipment were Air Serbia flights from Belgrade to Podgorica and Tivat.
This means that the entire preparation of the aircraft, from baggage handling to all accompanying operations on the apron, was carried out without emissions from the ground equipment.
This shows that sustainability in aviation is no longer a vision of the future, but a standard that can be implemented today.
Our ISAGO certification, one of the most recognized international standards for ground operations safety, confirms that we consistently apply these standards in practice.
text:
When a plane takes off, most passengers believe that the most demanding part of the journey has just begun. In reality, the most important work is already done. In the thirty minutes or so before takeoff, dozens of people, vehicles and sophisticated systems on the airport apron must operate in perfect coordination to ensure the flight is safe, punctual and efficient.

It is in this part of the airport, almost invisible to passengers, that one of the biggest transformations in the aviation industry is taking place today. Electric vehicles are replacing diesel-powered vehicles, artificial intelligence is improving operations, and virtual reality is becoming part of employee training. The goal is not just modernization, but safer, quieter, and more sustainable airports.

As the world's largest provider of ground handling services, Menzies Aviation operates at 349 airports in 62 countries, employs more than 65.000 people and handles over 5,3 million flights annually. Through a global sustainability strategy All In, the company is investing in the electrification of equipment, the digitalization of processes and the reduction of emissions, demonstrating that sustainability and operational excellence can go hand in hand.

What can such an experience mean for Montenegro, which is recording a continuous increase in the number of passengers and is facing important decisions about the future of its airports? We spoke to the general manager about this, as well as what the airports of the future look like. Menzies Aviation for Serbia and Montenegro, Anom Marojevic.

When an ordinary person looks at a plane through a terminal window, they mostly think about the flight, not the machines around them. Why do you say at Menzies that the real environmental and safety fight begins right there – on the apron?

Most passengers see the plane and think about their trip, but what happens around the aircraft in those 30 to 45 minutes before takeoff is just as important as the flight itself. During that short period, dozens of different vehicles and machines are simultaneously working around the plane, delivering luggage and cargo, supplying the plane with the necessary resources, and preparing it for the next flight.

All of these activities create noise and emissions that our employees, as well as passengers waiting to board, are exposed to every day. When you multiply that by the millions of flights that operate every day around the world, it becomes clear that a large part of the fight for cleaner air and more sustainable aviation is being fought right on the platform.

That is why the European Union, through the Green Agenda, is increasingly focusing on sustainable development and reducing emissions in all segments of aviation, not only during the flight but also in ground operations. As the country that has made the most progress in the process of accession to the European Union, Montenegro will increasingly align its standards with European sustainability and environmental protection policies in the coming years, so investing in cleaner technologies and modernizing ground handling will be not only a responsible business move, but also an expected direction of development.

That's why we believe that change must start on the ground. By investing in electrical equipment, modern technologies and more sustainable processes, we reduce emissions, improve working conditions and further increase the safety of operations. In aviation, we often say that safe flight does not begin when the plane takes off, but much earlier – on the platform, where every detail must be precisely planned and executed.

You are leading the process of electrifying ground handling equipment. How complex is that process and how far have you come?

Electrification of ground handling equipment is one of our most important strategic projects and a process that has been ongoing for years. It is not just about replacing vehicles, but about changing the way airport operations work – from charging infrastructure to work organization and employee training.

So far, we have introduced more than 628 new electric vehicles globally and invested over $200 million in equipment, so that today a quarter of our ground handling fleet is fully electric.

In Europe, we have gone a step further – more than half of our equipment is powered by electricity, and at some airports, the percentage exceeds 70 percent. The result is not only lower emissions. Electric equipment also means less noise, better working conditions for employees, a more pleasant environment for passengers and more efficient daily operations. This shows that sustainability and operational efficiency can and should go hand in hand.

How does all this work on a regional level? You mentioned that the first fully "electric" flights were carried out precisely to Montenegro?

Since March 2024, we have taken over ground operations at Belgrade Nikola Tesla Airport, as a strategic partner and joint venture with Air Serbia, and already today more than 80 percent of our equipment there operates on electric power.

We are particularly pleased that the first flights in the region to be fully serviced with electric ground equipment were Air Serbia flights from Belgrade to Podgorica and Tivat. This means that the entire preparation of the aircraft, from baggage handling to all accompanying operations on the apron, was carried out without emissions from the ground equipment. This shows that such solutions are not a plan for the future, but that they are already successfully functioning in our region today.

This could be particularly significant for Montenegro and I believe that the implementation of such solutions would be a natural next step, especially considering that Montenegro is the first ecological state in the world defined by the Constitution and that as a future member of the European Union it is intensively harmonizing its regulations with European standards of sustainable development and the Green Agenda. Electrification of ground equipment at airports represents a concrete way to simultaneously reduce emissions and noise, improve the working conditions of employees and further increase the efficiency and safety of operations. This shows that sustainability in aviation is no longer a vision of the future, but a standard that can be implemented today.

On the road to zero emissions, is replacing diesel engines with electric batteries the only solution?

Electrification is an important step, but it is not the only solution. The path to zero emissions involves a combination of different technologies and approaches. We are aware that not all airport equipment can be replaced with electric immediately, so we are working in parallel on other ways to reduce emissions.

Where electric propulsion is not yet an option, we use alternative fuels with a lower carbon footprint, such as hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO). In 2025, we increased its use by 50 percent compared to the previous year, using more than two million liters of this renewable fuel in our operations.

At the same time, we are increasing the use of electricity from renewable sources and investing in solar energy projects, because we believe that sustainability cannot be built through a single measure, but through a series of concrete steps.

Collaboration with partners on the development of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) is particularly important. Through our partnership with FlyORO, we are working to improve the way SAF is stored, blended and distributed at airports, making its application simpler and more accessible. This is an important step towards reducing emissions in aviation, especially in segments where fully electric solutions do not yet exist.

You have also introduced artificial intelligence (AI) and virtual reality (VR) into ground handling. What does that look like in practice?

Technology today is not an add-on to business – it is one of the key tools for greater safety, efficiency and quality of service. Our ISAGO certification, one of the most recognized international standards for ground operations safety, confirms that we consistently apply these standards in practice.

We use artificial intelligence to improve cargo operations and data management, which has almost completely digitized processes, eliminated large amounts of paperwork, and significantly accelerated the flow of goods. AI allows us to make faster decisions, improve process visibility, and reduce the possibility of human error.

At the same time, virtual reality has completely changed the way we train our employees. Before they step onto the platform and work alongside aircraft, our employees undergo realistic simulations of various operational situations in a safe virtual environment. This way, they gain risk-free experience, are better prepared for real-world challenges, and at the same time further increase the safety of employees, passengers, and aircraft.

What are your long-term goals when it comes to environmental protection?

Sustainability for us is not a one- or two-year project, but a long-term business strategy. That's why our goals are defined and independently verified through the global Science Based Targets (SBTi) initiative, which confirms that they are aligned with scientific recommendations for combating climate change.

We have committed to halving greenhouse gas emissions from our operations and energy consumption by 2030, while reducing emissions across our value chain. Our ultimate goal is to achieve net zero emissions across all business segments by 2045.

At the same time, sustainability for us is not just a matter of technology and numbers. We also invest in nature protection through reforestation projects, as well as in socially responsible initiatives and partnerships with local communities. We believe that successful business must leave a positive mark – not only in the economy, but also in the communities and environment in which we operate.

Menzies is a company with a tradition that dates back almost two centuries. What does this combination of history and modern technology bring to the context of Montenegro?

We have been in business since 1833, today we have more than 65.000 employees at 349 airports and we serve more than 5,3 million flights annually. Few companies in the aviation industry can combine almost two centuries of experience with the most modern technologies and the highest operational standards.

For Montenegro, which is recording an increase in the number of passengers year after year, this means a partner who thinks not only about today's needs, but also about how to prepare airports for future growth. We want to invest in infrastructure, introduce modern electrical equipment and digital solutions that improve efficiency and sustainability, but above all, invest in people through training local staff and developing a new generation of experts in the aviation industry.

We believe that Montenegro can gain much more from an investor, a long-term partner who will contribute to the development of tourism, better international connectivity of the country, and the creation of new opportunities for the economy and citizens.

What would Menzies' experience and global expertise specifically mean for travelers, employees, and the Montenegrin economy?

Our experience primarily means transferring knowledge and proven solutions that we apply daily at hundreds of airports around the world. There is no universal model that can be simply copied, but there are standards of safety, efficiency and quality that have been proven in practice and which we want to adapt to the needs of Montenegro.

For passengers, this would mean faster and simpler procedures, more reliable operations and a better quality experience at the airport. For employees, the opportunity to work with modern equipment, continuous training and the possibility of professional development within a global company. For airlines, this means a partner that can meet the demands of modern air traffic, while for Montenegro it would mean new investments, knowledge transfer, development of local professionals and support for the green transition through investments in sustainable technologies, electrification of equipment and modernization of airport operations.

We believe that the airports in Podgorica and Tivat have the potential to function according to the highest international standards. At the same time, we are convinced that the development of aviation today cannot be viewed separately from the strategic goals of the state – strengthening the competitiveness of the economy, sustainable development, improving tourism and European integration. That is why we believe that investing in modern airport operations represents an investment in the long-term competitiveness of Montenegro. Our goal is not only to improve everyday operations, but also to contribute, together with local partners, to the construction of a modern, sustainable and efficient aviation system that will be aligned with the highest European standards and create long-term value for passengers, the economy and the state.

Finally – what is the main message for passengers flying from Podgorica or Tivat, and what is Menzies' vision for Montenegro?

Most passengers will never think about what happens around the plane before takeoff – and that's a sign that we're doing our job right. When everything is organized properly, the passenger only sees what's important to them: that the flight starts on time, that their luggage has arrived with them, and that they feel safe.

Our vision for Montenegro is exactly that – for the airports in Podgorica and Tivat to be places where top-notch organization, safety and sustainability are a given. We want to bring the experience we have built over almost two centuries and applied at hundreds of airports around the world, but always with respect for local needs and the people who live and work here.

In the end, aviation is not just infrastructure and technology. It connects families, opens doors to tourism, business and new opportunities. If one day passengers from Podgorica or Tivat talk only about a nice trip, and not about waiting, crowds or problems at the airport, we will consider ourselves successful.

text:
NorSAF, the Latvian company developing the Baltic's largest sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) project, has signed a memorandum of understanding with UK clean-tech firm Nova Pangaea Technologies to develop an advanced ethanol plant in Latvia.

The plant would use locally sourced wood waste to produce ethanol, which would then supply NorSAF's planned SAF facility in Liepāja.

Nova Pangaea's REFNOVA technology converts waste biomass, including woody and agricultural residues that are plentiful in Latvia, into ethanol and biochar. The biochar is a co-product that permanently captures carbon, which the company says makes the process carbon negative. The ethanol can then be converted to SAF through the alcohol-to-jet pathway as part of NorSAF's production plans.

The partners are positioning the project as a response to Europe's reliance on imported feedstocks. EU rules require aviation fuel suppliers to raise the SAF share at EU airports from 2 per cent in 2025 to 6 per cent in 2030 and 20 per cent by 2035.

Much of Europe's current SAF is produced domestically using HEFA technology, but that route depends heavily on imported feedstocks such as used cooking oil.

Around 85 per cent of Europe's SAF feedstocks already come from overseas, with China alone accounting for 61 per cent.

The partners argue that agricultural and forestry residues offer a regional alternative, particularly in countries like Latvia where such resources are abundant.

Janis Kisiels, founder and board member of NorSAF, said: "Europe cannot strengthen its energy security simply by reducing fossil-fuel imports. We also need to build the industrial capacity to produce the clean fuels that will replace them. Right now, Europe is dangerously dependent on overseas feedstocks like used cooking oil, leaving our aviation sector vulnerable to international supply chain shocks. By tapping into Europe's own abundant waste resources, particularly those available in the Baltic region, we can build a resilient, domestic supply chain from the ground up. Our partnership with Nova Pangaea is a crucial milestone in developing that strategic capability right here in Latvia, ensuring our future SAF production is sustainable, secure, and locally anchored."

Jonathan Wood, chief commercial officer of Nova Pangaea, said: "This strategic collaboration will ensure we have carbon-negative ethanol to feed NorSAF's SAF project, using locally sourced biomass waste. This is a blueprint for the type of partnerships we need to scale SAF production in Europe and all regions of the world, enhancing energy security, building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and economic growth while reducing fossil-fuel emissions. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), there is sufficient waste biomass available in Europe to produce enough SAF to meet Europe's ambitious SAF targets for 2050."

The Latvian project has historical roots. Nova Pangaea's technology is based on research carried out at the Latvian State Institute of Wood Chemistry in Riga, before further development and demonstration work in the UK, where the company has worked with British Airways and LanzaJet on Project Speedbird, a UK government-supported initiative to produce SAF from non-food agricultural and woody biomass.

NorSAF currently operates a liquid oil and chemical product storage and transshipment terminal in the Liepāja Special Economic Zone. It is developing a SAF and eSAF production facility at the Port of Liepāja using KBR's PureSAF technology, originally developed by Swedish Biofuels, with production expected to begin in 2031.

The proposed Latvian ethanol project complements that plan by exploring whether part of the required raw material can come from forestry and agricultural waste in the region. Avia Solutions Group, the world's largest ACMI provider, is a partner on the project, giving NorSAF access to aviation infrastructure including its subsidiary Baltic Ground Services, which has experience in SAF supply and distribution.

text:
SAF becomes an EU strategic energy-security asset

Geopolitical instability is repositioning sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from a decarbonisation product into a strategic energy-security asset. However, Europe’s fragmented traceability rules and pipeline regulations could prevent supply chains from scaling efficiently. Furthermore, senior vice president for business development in the Netherlands Nikki Schutte argues that harmonised EU rules are needed to reduce logistics costs and unlock investment as SAF demand is projected to rise from 62,000 barrels per day in 2026 to 80,000 barrels per day in 2027, while ReFuelEU targets increase from 2% of EU aviation fuel in 2025 to 70% by 2050.

The immediate effect is likely to be stronger political and commercial support for SAF as a hedge against disruptions to conventional jet-fuel supply, although the main constraints on market growth remain. Moreover, major ports like Rotterdam and other import hubs could become large-scale blending and certification centres. At the same time, airports and airlines increasingly compete for verified environmental attributes rather than physically delivered SAF molecules. This may lower system costs and improve resilience, but it also increases dependence on credible registries, auditing, and anti-double-counting controls.

Strategically, SAF policy is becoming industrial policy as jurisdictions offering stable mandates, flexible logistics, and reliable certification will attract producers, storage capacity, and capital.

The Netherlands’ voluntary blending experience suggests incentives can accelerate adoption, but long-term volume growth will remain mandate-led rather than purely market-led.

China turns copper merger review into supply-security leverage

China reportedly demands guaranteed copper-concentrate supplies to approve Anglo American’s $54 billion merger with Teck Resources. Its antitrust regulator is negotiating remedies after smelters raised concerns amid China’s worst feedstock shortage in decades.

Although the combined group would hold only about 5% of global copper supply, China’s role as a major buyer gives it effective veto power.

The case shows resource-hungry countries increasingly using merger reviews to secure critical-mineral supply for the energy transition.

Big oil challenges climate liability cases as US Supreme Court opens new term

The US Supreme Court will open its new term by hearing ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy’s attempt to dismiss Boulder, Colorado’s climate-liability lawsuit. Boulder alleges the companies contributed to climate change and misled the public, seeking damages for infrastructure repairs, environmental harm, emergency management, and public-health costs.

The companies argue that federal laws like the Clean Air Act prevent state-based claims from proceeding. The case could determine the future of nearly 60 similar lawsuits brought by US states and local governments seeking billions from fossil-fuel producers. A ruling for the companies could eliminate many cases, while a ruling for Boulder would expand climate-liability risks.

Algebris Investments has acquired Spanish renewable energy advisory and asset-management firm Vector Renewables from Nadara through its Green Transition Fund, marking the fund’s first international acquisition.

The deal strengthens Algebris’s energy-transition portfolio and international presence while giving Vector greater independence to expand globally and develop technologies such as battery-energy-storage systems and hybrid projects.
