Spain joins the UK and other countries in opposing EU rules on carbon emissions in an effort to fundamentally change global flight economics. Airlines face rising costs as carbon-free emission permits disappear from European airspace. Spain joins the UK and other countries in opposing EU rules on carbon emissions because of stringent environmental guidelines that require immediate operational modifications. Major airlines are now required to buy every emission allowance at market price. Passengers face rising ticket prices. Airline companies use clean fuel and modernize aging aircraft to reduce costs. This landmark measure is set to change how international airline companies comply, maintain operating margins and ensure long-term sustainability.

The implementation of full market auctioning of emissions under the EU ETS has completely overhauled airline economics, shifting environmental compliance from a minor regulatory issue to a major balance sheet item. Global carriers operating in European airspace need to buy 100 percent of required compliance units in the present system, which has forced airline executives to rethink network planning, pricing schemes and asset management strategies.

How does full carbon auctioning reshape airline financial engineering?

The elimination of free carbon allocations forces commercial airline treasuries to treat emission allowances as an unavoidable, variable input cost comparable to jet fuel procurement. Financial controllers must now actively hedge carbon unit price volatility alongside traditional petroleum futures to protect operating margins across regional networks. This structural shift disproportionately penalizes short-haul high-frequency routes where per-passenger emissions intensity remains significantly higher relative to long-haul alternatives. Airline revenue management systems are consequently embedding real-time carbon surcharges directly into ticket pricing matrices for European itineraries. Investors and lessors closely scrutinize an operator’s fleet age and route mix to evaluate long-term exposure to these escalating regulatory liabilities. Companies lacking capital access for rapid fleet modernization face severe cash flow contractions under the fully phased-in cap-and-trade regime. Consequently, strategic asset allocation decisions are increasingly dictated by a carrier’s ability to minimize carbon overhead per available seat kilometer.

Fleet financing agreements now incorporate strict environmental covenants tied directly to an airline’s projected compliance costs and emissions trajectory. Banking syndicates demand granular transparency regarding carbon exposure before extending favorable credit terms for aircraft acquisitions or major lease restructurings. Older, less fuel-efficient airframes are suffering from accelerated depreciation schedules as secondary market demand shifts toward modern, lower-emission variants. Asset lessors routinely re-evaluate residual value assumptions for older narrowbody fleets due to the compounding financial burden of purchasing unallocated allowances. Airlines are forced to accelerate capital expenditure plans to phase out legacy turbine engines well ahead of previous corporate timelines. This intense financial pressure transforms environmental compliance into a central driver of corporate restructuring and competitive market differentiation. Executive boards must continuously balance short-term profitability against the absolute necessity of green technology investments.

For full official documentation on regional compliance and trading rules, consult the European Commission EU ETS Framework and the UK Government ETS Aviation Guidance.

What operational modifications optimize compliance under strict emissions caps?

Flight dispatchers and operational control centers now integrate real-time carbon tracking software directly into daily flight planning and routing optimization algorithms. Ground operations are heavily scrutinized to minimize auxiliary power unit runtime and eliminate inefficient taxiing delays across congested European hub airports. Flight crews receive specialized training focused on continuous descent operations and optimal altitude selection to shave fractions of fuel burn per trip. Every single kilogram of unnecessary weight aboard commercial aircraft is systematically removed to drive down cumulative emissions totals. Maintenance engineering teams execute frequent engine washes and aerodynamic modifications to preserve peak fuel efficiency across active fleets. These meticulous operational adjustments provide immediate, albeit incremental, relief against soaring monthly allowance purchasing requirements. Dispatch procedures also factor in strict non-carbon dioxide emissions monitoring parameters established under emerging European regulatory reporting mandates.

Collaborative digital platforms allow airlines to share best practices for minimizing environmental compliance exposure across shared European airspace corridors. Ground handling agents adopt electric-powered ramp equipment to reduce stationary emissions footprints at major international terminal gates. Maintenance schedules are rigorously optimized to ensure turbine performance remains at peak operating levels throughout heavy operational cycles. Operational risk managers conduct continuous audits to verify that internal data collection workflows align precisely with statutory monitoring standards. Flight planners leverage advanced meteorological forecasting tools to sidestep headwinds and reduce unnecessary fuel consumption on marginal routes. These comprehensive adjustments ensure that every department within an airline contributes directly to minimizing regulatory financial exposure. Operational excellence thus serves as the primary operational defense against escalating market-driven carbon costs.

“Spain aligns with the UK and other nations on aviation carbon rules to reshape global flight economics forever. Experts warn that eliminating free carbon permits will permanently alter ticket pricing structures across every major European corridor. Airlines must now absorb massive operational costs or pass them directly to passengers. Industry leaders emphasize that fleet modernization and sustainable aviation fuel adoption are no longer optional corporate goals. Instead, they represent absolute survival strategies in a ruthless market. As regulatory scrutiny intensifies, proactive compliance will separate thriving global carriers from those struggling under heavy environmental financial burdens.”

— Anup Kumar Keshan, Founder and Editor-in-Chief, Travel And Tour World

Why do multi-layered compliance frameworks create international administrative friction?

The simultaneous enforcement of the regional EU ETS and the global Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation creates complex compliance burdens for foreign operators. International carriers flying into European hubs must navigate overlapping reporting jurisdictions, disparate verification timelines, and distinct offset purchasing criteria. Foreign government ministries frequently argue that regional mandates impose unfair extraterritorial financial penalties on non-European commercial aviation businesses. Legal teams spend countless hours reconciling conflicting data requirements to ensure compliance with both domestic and international statutes. Industry trade associations continue lobbying for unified global standards to eliminate costly administrative redundancies and reduce regulatory friction. Diplomatic channels remain active as nations negotiate compromise solutions to prevent potential international trade retaliation and airspace disputes. Transparent data-sharing protocols are gradually being established to bridge the operational gap between regional regulators and global oversight bodies.

Developing economies express ongoing concern that rigid carbon pricing frameworks restrict their future economic connectivity and tourism growth potential. Foreign legacy carriers operating lucrative transatlantic legs must absorb these layered compliance overheads while competing against non-regulated regional alternatives. Strategic legal planning becomes indispensable for multinational airlines managing multi-jurisdictional tax and environmental liabilities simultaneously. Regulatory authorities maintain that regional urgency remains fully justified while global consensus mechanisms evolve at a slower pace. Harmonization working groups meet regularly to align carbon accounting methodologies and prevent double-counting across international borders. The aviation sector adapts incrementally to this intricate regulatory reality through robust compliance infrastructure and proactive diplomatic engagement. Strategic foresight and advanced data management systems remain the ultimate prerequisites for surviving this complex era of global environmental accountability.

Here is a detailed breakdown of how each of these four countries approaches and adapts to the European carbon trading and aviation sector revisions:

Spain manages massive inbound and outbound tourism flows, anchored by major transport hubs like Madrid-Barajas and Barcelona-El Prat, alongside powerful airline groups like International Consolidated Airlines Group (IAG), which includes Iberia and Vueling. Spanish authorities and local carriers generally support the broader European decarbonization roadmap. However, tourism-dependent regions and airline executives frequently voice concerns over ticket price inflation and the risk of losing market share to non-EU transiting corridors. To offset full market auctioning costs, Spanish carriers are accelerating fleet modernization programs and leveraging EU ETS-backed modernization funds to secure and scale up sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) integration across their short- and medium-haul networks.

Centered around Amsterdam Airport Schiphol and flagship carrier KLM, the Netherlands acts as a premier European mega-hub heavily dependent on connecting global passenger traffic. The Dutch government strongly champions stringent European environmental regulations. At the same time, the country walks a delicate domestic tightrope, balancing strict airport capacity caps and local emissions/noise restrictions with the economic realities of maintaining its hub status. KLM faces immediate financial pressure from the complete phase-out of free allowances. In response, Dutch aviation stakeholders are aggressively deploying operational slot optimizations, investing in electric ground-handling equipment, and pioneering corporate SAF adoption across European routes.

Operating outside the European Union yet deeply entangled in European airspace through major hubs like London Heathrow, the UK maintains massive trans-European flight volumes driven by carriers like British Airways and easyJet. The UK closely mirrors many of the EU ETS stringency measures to prevent regulatory arbitrage and has explored mechanisms to link the UK ETS with the EU system. British authorities emphasize aligning carbon pricing to ensure domestic airlines remain competitive on overlapping routes. UK carriers operating flights to and within the EEA must navigate dual-market compliance tracking. To counter soaring carbon liabilities, the UK government has enforced strict domestic SAF blending mandates targeting 10% by 2030, compelling airlines to secure long-term alternative fuel supply contracts.

As a major non-European player with numerous long-haul flights over the Atlantic connecting Canada’s transport hubs with European entry points, Canadian carriers account for significant volumes of traffic between the two continents. At the same time, Canada has always promoted international regulation at the level of the UN, and the country’s transport sector representatives have voiced concerns regarding the unilateral imposition of carbon pricing on airlines by individual EU countries. Canadian carriers operating flights to the EEA have to track and report greenhouse gas emissions for each flight leg subject to the EU’s ETS and offset them if required. To reduce exposure to potential carbon costs imposed by the EU, Canadian carriers look to establish direct purchase links with regional SAF producers and optimize long-haul flight operations.

Spain backs UK and others on carbon rules for planes to create strict net-zero rules. The regional authorities canceled free allowances. This means that the airline companies are forced to buy back permits. This creates a financial push for more green fuel and modernization of aircraft.

Reasons why Spain supports the UK and other nations in terms of carbon regulations regarding the world of aviation includes the fact that the skies today require responsibility. The aviation industry managed to survive and grow as a result of quick adaptation, intelligent strategies, compliance, and an eye on sustainability.

L’aeromobile è configurato con 331 posti in tre classi: 34 in World Business Class, 26 in Premium Comfort e 271 in Economy. Tra le altre destinazioni del primo A350 durante la IATA Winter 2026 flight season figurano Montreal, Kilimanjaro, Dar es Salaam, Nairobi e Zanzibar.

Con questo traguardo, KLM si unisce ad Air France nell’elenco degli operatori dell’A350. Air France ha ricevuto il suo primo A350 nel 2019 e attualmente opera con 43 aeromobili di questo tipo.

Questa prima consegna fa seguito a ordini successivi effettuati da Air France-KLM, che hanno portato a un portafoglio ordini di 99 Airbus A350, sia in versione passeggeri che cargo, con diritti di acquisto per ulteriori 40 aeromobili. Ciò posiziona Air France-KLM tra i maggiori operatori al mondo di aeromobili della A350 family”, afferma Air France-KLM Group.

“Oggi è un traguardo importante per KLM e per il Gruppo, con entrambi i nostri network carriers che ora operano con aeromobili Airbus A350”, ha dichiarato Benjamin Smith, CEO di Air France-KLM. “Con l’introduzione dell’A350, KLM compie un ulteriore passo avanti nell’integrazione di aeromobili più silenziosi ed efficienti dal punto di vista dei consumi nella sua flotta a lungo raggio. Il nostro ingente investimento sottolinea il nostro sincero impegno nei confronti dei Paesi Bassi, della connettività olandese e nella costruzione di una KLM più forte per il futuro”.

“KLM prevede di ricevere un secondo A350-900 quest’anno e le consegne proseguiranno costantemente nei prossimi anni. Per dare un nome agli A350 della sua flotta, KLM ha scelto celebri opere d’arte olandesi. Il primo A350 si chiama ‘The Night Watch’ di Rembrandt van Rijn, forse il capolavoro più famoso dei Paesi Bassi, che attira visitatori da tutto il mondo al Rijksmuseum. Il secondo aereo si chiamerà ‘Girl with a Pearl Earring’.

Grazie alle più recenti innovazioni tecnologiche, l’Airbus A350 offre le migliori performance della sua categoria per le esigenze delle compagnie aeree del Gruppo. Rispetto agli aeromobili di precedente generazione, offre una riduzione del rumore del 40% e una riduzione del consumo di carburante del 25%.

Il rinnovo della flotta è la prima leva per ridurre le emissioni di CO2 e il rumore, con effetto immediato. Insieme all’utilizzo di Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF), a misure operative come l’eco-piloting e all’offerta di opzioni di viaggio intermodali ai clienti tramite il servizio Air+Rail, questo rappresenta uno dei pilastri del percorso di decarbonizzazione del Gruppo.

Entro il 2030, l’obiettivo di Air France-KLM è raggiungere una quota dell’80% di aeromobili di nuova generazione nella flotta del Gruppo, rispetto al 38% di luglio 2026.

Al 2 ottobre 2026, Air France-KLM opera una flotta di 593 aeromobili verso oltre 320 destinazioni in tutto il mondo”, conclude Air France-KLM Group.

text:
Ambani shared the proposal at a foundation-stone ceremony in Madanapalle on Friday (October 2). At the event, the state also launched two large agriculture-focused initiatives- the Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub and the Indian School of Agriculture (ISA).

Compressed biogas: Turning farm waste into fuel

Compressed biogas is a renewable fuel made by processing organic waste—such as crop residue, animal dung, food waste and other biomass—into methane-rich gas that can replace conventional natural gas in transport, industry and commercial use. By converting waste into energy and nutrient-rich bio-manure, CBG projects aim to reduce landfill and field burning, cut greenhouse gas emissions, and create new income streams for rural households.

Anant Ambani said, “Reliance Industries is grateful to the Government of Andhra Pradesh for the opportunity to invest Rs 1 lakh crore in the state to set up compressed biogas plants.”

A broader clean-energy and manufacturing push

Beyond CBG, Ambani said Reliance is investing in clean-energy projects in Rayalaseema and exploring opportunities in advanced manufacturing in the state. He cited government data indicating that Andhra Pradesh has approved 388 mega projects since June 2024, with total investment commitments above Rs 14 lakh crore and potential employment of almost 11 lakh people; about a third of that investment is expected to flow into the Rayalaseema region.

Reliance also said it would continue supporting the Indian School of Agriculture through “strategic investment, digital capabilities, technical expertise and industry partnerships”. “Today, we are not just laying foundation stones. We are laying the foundations for rural enterprise, stronger villages, a more sustainable India, and most importantly, for improving the lives of our farmers,” Ambani said.

Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub: A Rs 40,000–1 lakh crore farm push

The Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, announced alongside the ISA, is designed to promote technology-driven horticulture in a historically drought-prone region. Reports describe it as part of a larger plan with an overall investment of around Rs 1 lakh crore, including roughly Rs 40,000 crore from the Centre (under schemes such as Purvodaya) and about Rs 60,000 crore expected from private investors and the state.

Indian School of Agriculture: AI, drones and farm CEOs

The Indian School of Agriculture in Madanapalle is envisioned as a training and innovation hub that blends modern technology with traditional farming knowledge. Ambani said the school would use tools such as artificial intelligence, drone-based crop monitoring, precision irrigation, robotics and price intelligence to help farmers improve yields and incomes.

“Here in this School, Artificial Intelligence (AI) will meet the Traditional Intelligence of Bharat’s hard-working Kisans,” he said.

Virtual classrooms and a farmer platform

Reliance’s telecom arm, Jio, is expected to work with the ISA to deliver training to millions of farmers in Indian languages through virtual classrooms in villages. The idea is to train rural youth as digitally enabled extension workers who can support local farmers with technology and market information.

Ambani also pointed to Jio Krishi, a platform developed by Jio with products and services aimed at farmers, and noted Reliance’s bio-energy R&D centre in Jamnagar. He said the group would explore cooperation between the ISA and Vantara’s proposed university for wildlife and veterinary sciences, to broaden career options in agriculture and allied fields.

The Rs 1 lakh crore CBG investment plan is expected to create more than 3 lakh jobs, especially in rural areas, and generate nearly Rs 60,000 crore in state revenue over several decades. It could also give farmers new markets for crop residue and organic waste, while producing cleaner fuel and bio-manure. Along with the proposed horticulture hub and ISA, the plan aims to link agriculture with clean energy and technology.

text:
Cardano's ADA token is trading near $0.242, pinned almost exactly to its 200-day moving average, despite two announcements this week that would likely have jolted other digital assets higher. The price action raises a pointed question for traders: why has news that Brazil's state oil company is testing the network and that the Cardano Foundation has secured a partner in Japan failed to translate into meaningful buying pressure?

The answer, according to market participants and technical analysts, lies in the nature of the announcements themselves. Both are exploratory, research-stage initiatives with no near-term revenue implications, and neither creates immediate demand for ADA. The broader crypto market has also offered little tailwind, with Bitcoin moving less than one percent over the past seven days.

What Petrobras and Pacific Meta actually announced

Petrobras, in collaboration with the Ledger Lab at PUC-Rio university, has developed two applications on Cardano. The first makes the environmental benefit of sustainable aviation fuel transferable as a token, allowing an airline or passenger to acquire the certificate even when the physical fuel is burned elsewhere. The token is designed to be redeemable only once, preventing the same certificate from being sold twice. The second application tracks the production, transport and consumption of Diesel R, the company's renewable diesel product.

Both projects are explicitly at the research stage. No party involved has provided a timeline for regular commercial operation, and there is no indication of how many transactions the applications would generate or whether any meaningful amount of ADA would be required to run them.

The second piece of news arrived on October 1, when the Cardano Foundation announced a partnership with Pacific Meta, a Tokyo-based blockchain incubator that will help Japanese companies build applications on the network. Japan is not a new market for Cardano, which has maintained a substantial following there since its 2017 launch. According to data from Santiment cited by CoinCentral, the number of daily active addresses nearly doubled after the announcement to more than 27,500.

Yet the market's response has been muted. In the 24 hours following the Japan report, ADA's high reached only about $0.2585, essentially matching the level it touched on September 25 when it closed at $0.2586.

The technical picture

ADA has been balancing on its 200-day moving average for twelve consecutive days. Since September 21, every daily close has landed between $0.2385 and $0.2586, a band of roughly eight percent. This compression suggests the token is coiling for a directional move, but the direction remains unresolved.

The levels that matter are clearly defined. On the upside, $0.26 is the line to watch. A daily close above that threshold would mark the first sign that the recent news is finally reaching the price and could turn the current sideways phase into a breakout. On the downside, the 50-day moving average sits at $0.22, and the lows from August 30 and September 15 were around $0.195. The recovery that lifted ADA by roughly a third into late September started from that zone.

Momentum indicators are split. The daily 14-period RSI was 59.5 on October 2, placing it in bullish-but-not-overbought territory. The 12-day EMA stood at $0.2434, above the 26-day EMA at $0.2328, and ADA was trading above both its 50-day and 200-day simple moving averages. However, MACD readings from different data providers have shown conflicting signals, with one October 2 reading showing a narrow bearish crossover while an October 1 reading showed the opposite.

Derivatives data adds another layer of caution. Futures open interest fell 9 percent week over week to about $1.81 billion, and large holders reportedly sold around 90 million ADA since September 20, according to Coin Edition. These flows do not negate the spot-market response to the Petrobras news, but they complicate the case that the announcement alone has created broad, durable buying pressure.

The distinction between narrative and demand is central to understanding ADA's price action. News of this kind functions closer to sentiment than to actual buying pressure. For the price to move meaningfully, traders need evidence of either sustained spot accumulation or a shift in the broader market environment that gives smaller coins room to run.

The macro backdrop

The same week that Cardano's news failed to move its price, the crypto industry's attention was also focused on Seoul, where the CONNECT by Cointelegraph event during Korea Blockchain Week brought together investors, builders and traditional finance executives to discuss the forces shaping digital asset markets.

Arthur Hayes, chief investment officer at Maelstrom, delivered one of the more provocative assessments. He argued that the scale of capital required for AI infrastructure—particularly data centers—runs alongside a broader environment in which traditional funding avenues are stretched. AI companies need trillions of dollars to finance the infrastructure behind their services even as the market pushes prices downward, he said. That mismatch, in his view, narrows the options available to policymakers and points toward monetary expansion as the likely outcome.

"They've not really given themselves a lot of options other than print money and make it less bad," Hayes said.

He also floated the possibility that China could shift from what he described as an "austerity lite" approach to more substantial stimulus. If such a pivot occurs, he suggested it could reawaken appetite for scarce assets—an idea that matters for crypto because digital assets have increasingly traded alongside broader liquidity expectations.

Hayes was also watching indicators of financial stress in Europe, including credit-default swaps referencing BNP Paribas and spreads tied to French government bonds. "I think the money printing will essentially happen at some point, but that's sort of a slow motion train wreck happening underneath the surface," he said.

Wall Street's onchain push still runs through customer relationships

A recurring theme at CONNECT was that traditional finance's entry into blockchain markets may not eliminate middlemen—it may simply shift where value accrues. Catrina Wang, general partner at Portal Ventures, argued that banks and asset managers bring established customer bases into blockchain markets, giving them an edge over companies that must build investor trust from scratch. She summarized the logic with a variation of an "aggregation" theme associated with tech analyst Ben Thompson: whoever holds the customer relationship tends to capture the economics.

"Whoever owns the customer relationship owns the economics," Wang said.

Todd McDonald, co-founder of R3, added that public blockchains can provide institutions a path to customers outside their existing private-network footprint. R3 previously centered its business on private financial networks through its Corda platform, before announcing a collaboration in May 2025 to connect institutions and their assets to Solana's public chain.

Justin Kugel, executive vice president of growth at World Liberty Financial, said the tradeoffs investors face—deciding where to allocate funds and how much risk to take—create demand for intermediaries, despite crypto's original promise to reduce reliance on traditional gatekeepers. Many users do not want to actively manage assets or perform deep risk assessment for each investment, he said, pointing to centralized exchanges as providing a level of perceived protection that can reduce the operational burden for non-experts.

"Maybe there's a reason why there are so many middlemen in TradFi," Kugel said.

Stablecoins and the yield question

Franklin Templeton's Chetan Karkhanis, senior vice president of digital asset client engagement, said the firm has no plans to issue its own stablecoin. Instead, it wants its tokenized money market funds to serve as the investment income engine—framing the offering as a "yield layer" that can sit alongside payment tokens.

"Let us be the yield layer," Karkhanis said.

He also noted operational realities: the firm's fund subscriptions and redemptions generally still require fiat. While some stablecoin-related conversions exist, he argued that these options need to be more broadly available across the industry to make stablecoin-based workflows practical at scale. In June, Franklin Templeton announced a partnership with MoonPay enabling eligible institutional investors to move between supported stablecoins and its tokenized money market funds through onchain transactions.

Haonan Li, co-founder and CEO of stablecoin foreign-exchange platform Codex, said demand for stablecoin payments is growing along trade routes connecting Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa with Asia. He described the pattern as manufactured goods flowing east to west while funds move west to east.

Treasury strategies hinge on liquidity

The conference also addressed corporate crypto treasuries and the practical constraints that often get overlooked when companies consider exposure to digital assets. Ilya Podoynitsyn, co-founder and CEO of FinHarbor, said companies considering crypto treasury strategies need cash that can be committed for longer periods without disrupting everyday operations. Without that excess liquidity, he argued, firms should proceed carefully.

"If you don't have that excess liquidity for doing that, you need to think very carefully before entering the market," Podoynitsyn said.

He cautioned against copying a strategy from another company without adjusting for differences in balance sheets, liquidity needs and risk tolerance. Even experienced finance teams, he suggested, may lack specific expertise in onchain liquidity and the transaction approval processes required for execution.

Michael Camarda, chief development officer at Ethereum treasury company SharpLink, addressed a question familiar to public-company investors: whether a listed treasury firm with spare cash should allocate it toward more crypto or instead repurchase shares trading below net asset value. Increasing ETH holdings per share can be accomplished in two ways, he said—buying back shares to spread existing Ether across fewer shares, or purchasing additional Ether to increase the total held by the firm. SharpLink's institutional investors prioritized ETH holdings per share, while retail investors were more responsive to headline-driven announcements of large Ether purchases, he said. The company used both levers to appeal to each group.

What to watch next

For Cardano, the next big step is technical rather than commercial. The fourth quarter of 2026 roadmap calls for completion of the first stage of Leios, an extension intended to raise the network's throughput. November is the announced target for production operation of the alternative node Amaru. Dates like these have a record of slipping at Cardano, but they represent the next occasions on which the project can demonstrate whether developers and users are following through.

For traders, the immediate focus remains on the price levels. A daily close above $0.26 would be the first sign that the Petrobras and Japan news is finally reaching the price. A close below $0.22 would suggest the opposite. With roughly 18 percent between those two levels, position sizing should account for the range.

For the broader crypto market, the macro questions raised in Seoul—whether policymakers expand liquidity, how traditional finance distributes tokenized products, and who supplies yield in the stablecoin ecosystem—will likely matter more than any single project announcement. Cardano's sideways trading this week is a reminder that in a market still waiting for its next directional catalyst, even credible enterprise adoption news can struggle to move the needle.

title: SAF Uptake Grows Across Aviation - Shape Tomorrow
description:
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) use in the UK has more than doubled in 2026, with new government figures showing that 291.7 million litres had been supplied under the UK’s SAF Mandate by the beginning of September.

For logistics and supply chain businesses, these developments show how the conversation around aviation emissions is moving from commitments towards actual fuel procurement.

text:
Sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) use in the UK has more than doubled in 2026, with new government figures showing that 291.7 million litres had been supplied under the UK’s SAF Mandate by the beginning of September. The provisional data represents 3.92% of aviation fuel reported under the mandate so far this year, showing how quickly SAF use is beginning to grow as the UK moves further into its new regulatory framework.

The figures, published by the Department for Transport (DfT) on 17 September, are based on information available up to 1 September and remain provisional, so the final figure for 2026 will be higher once the full year’s data is reported. Even at this stage, the increase compared with 2025 shows that SAF is becoming a more significant part of the UK aviation fuel mix, with suppliers facing increasing requirements to bring lower-carbon fuels into the market.

The UK SAF Mandate came into force in January 2025, requiring fuel suppliers to provide an increasing proportion of sustainable aviation fuel over time. The mandate started with a requirement equivalent to 2% of total UK jet fuel demand in 2025, rising to 10% by 2030 and 22% by 2040. For 2026, the main obligation has increased to 3.6%, meaning the industry is already working towards a higher level of SAF use as the UK moves towards its longer-term aviation decarbonisation targets.

The increase is particularly important because aviation remains one of the harder areas of transport to decarbonise through direct electrification. SAF can be used in existing aircraft and airport fuel infrastructure when blended with conventional jet fuel, giving airlines and freight operators a way to reduce the emissions associated with flying while other technologies continue to develop. Under the UK mandate, eligible SAF must meet sustainability requirements and deliver at least a 40% greenhouse gas emissions reduction, although the actual reduction depends on the fuel pathway and feedstock used.

The government is also working to support the development of a larger domestic SAF market. Its proposed revenue certainty mechanism is designed to give producers greater confidence to invest in new UK production facilities, while the government has recognised that significantly more SAF will be needed as the mandate increases and demand for lower-carbon aviation fuel grows.

This shift is not limited to the UK. In the US, FedEx has announced agreements expected to secure more than 20 million gallons of neat SAF across five airports through the end of 2027. The agreements cover Newark, Oakland, Miami, JFK and Dallas Fort Worth, with SAF expected to be supplied at blend ratios of between 30% and 50%, depending on the location.

The agreements build on FedEx’s existing SAF procurement, with the company having secured around 5 million gallons of neat SAF through agreements beginning in 2025. FedEx says this resulted in 16.5 million gallons of blended SAF being deployed across five US airports, and it is targeting alternative fuel blends for 30% of its jet fuel by 2030.

For logistics and supply chain businesses, these developments show how the conversation around aviation emissions is moving from commitments towards actual fuel procurement. SAF is not a single solution to aviation’s emissions challenge, and its impact depends on factors such as how the fuel is produced, the feedstock used and the emissions associated with its full lifecycle. There are also questions around cost, availability and whether production can grow quickly enough to meet rising demand.

The direction of travel is becoming clearer, however. The UK’s growing SAF supply, alongside procurement commitments from major international logistics operators such as FedEx, points to a market that is beginning to move beyond individual trials and towards larger-scale use. As mandates become more ambitious and companies make longer-term commitments, the pressure will increase on fuel producers, infrastructure providers and the wider aviation supply chain to scale SAF while maintaining the sustainability standards needed to deliver genuine emissions reductions.

As the logistics industry continues to look for practical ways to tackle Scope 3 emissions, these are the conversations that matter. Hear from industry experts, explore real-world solutions and be part of the conversation. title: Oil retains systemic leverage as economies decarbonize | Communications Sustainability
description:
The transition strategy question then is how economies maintain and grow essential functions while reducing dependence on liquid fuels.
Emergency fuel measures should be product-specific, time-limited and tied to essential services.
Oil-flow risk is also macrofinancial risk.
It is the capacity to sustain essential functions when international liquid-fuel flows are constrained.
These tests should identify essential fuel uses, product-specific reserve needs, rapidly scalable substitutes and emergency measures with explicit expiry conditions.
text:
Oil circulates through a tightly coupled network of production, shipping, refining, storage, distribution, and finance. Under stable conditions, this network delivers impressive scale and liquidity. Under disruption, the same connectivity can spread stress quickly across markets1.

The transition strategy question then is how economies maintain and grow essential functions while reducing dependence on liquid fuels. Figure 2 translates this into four checks for transition planning.

Oil-security planning also needs guardrails. Emergency fuel measures should be product-specific, time-limited and tied to essential services. Public support for storage, refining flexibility or local supply should include expiry dates, methane controls, decommissioning obligations and a declining-demand test. New or upgraded assets should be screened for stranded-asset risk, declining utilization and credible retirement or repurposing pathways. The IEA warns that net-zero transitions raise stranded-asset risk, especially for refineries and liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities. Resilience assessments should prioritize demand reduction and strengthening buffers and logistics, and only then consider supply-side options.

Transition plans should classify oil use by function and substitution time: essential uses that cannot be replaced quickly; uses amenable to targeted substitution; and discretionary uses that can be curtailed during crises. Emergency services, hospitals, food logistics, water systems and priority freight belong in the first group. Urban bus fleets, municipal vehicles, port equipment, short-haul freight and backup generators belong in the second. This classification would assist crisis policy to move from blunt fuel subsidies and payouts to targeted lifelines.

Oil-flow risk is also macrofinancial risk. Higher oil prices can add to inflation, weaken currencies, increase subsidy costs and raise sovereign borrowing costs3,6,7. These effects are especially consequential in import-dependent economies, where fuel bills compete with food, health, infrastructure and debt service. Energy planners and finance authorities should therefore jointly stress-test the effects of oil-flow disruption. Financial authorities could complement existing climate scenarios with short-horizon oil-deliverability shocks involving product shortages, freight-cost spikes, currency depreciation and subsidy stress14.

Investors and lenders should reflect this in project appraisals. Electrifying buses, ports, municipal fleets, short-haul freight and backup power can reduce both emissions and vulnerability to disruptions in fuel supplies. Current sustainable-finance frameworks tend to recognize the first benefit more clearly than the second. For example, the European Union Taxonomy and Green Bond Principles focus on environmental outcomes15,16. Yet projects that reduce dependence on liquid fuels can also improve resilience to fuel-supply disruptions. This resilience benefit should be considered alongside climate benefits in investment and financing decisions.

Energy security in a decarbonizing economy is therefore defined neither by installed low-carbon capacity nor by domestic fossil-fuel production alone. It is the capacity to sustain essential functions when international liquid-fuel flows are constrained.

Additional local supply or refining flexibility should be considered only where demand reduction, electrification, product reserves, import diversity or regional cooperation cannot close a defined continuity gap at comparable speed and reliability. Such measures are transitional safeguards, not a rationale for preserving fossil-fuel dependence or weakening long-term decarbonization goals. Recognizing oil-flow vulnerabilities should instead strengthen the case for faster substitution.

The objective is not absolute energy independence, but managed exposure to fuel-flow risk. Economies should rigorously identify which fuel flows are essential, how long they can operate without them, which substitutes can scale quickly, and which emergency measures should be implemented in what order.

Decarbonization will progressively weaken oil’s leverage as essential services reduce their dependence on liquid fuels. That leverage can nevertheless persist while critical functions remain tied to vulnerable supply networks. Energy security should therefore be assessed not only through renewable capacity and fuel-supply-chain diversity, but also through the ability to sustain essential functions under oil-flow stress.

The practical next step is clear: incorporate oil-deliverability stress tests into transition planning. These tests should identify essential fuel uses, product-specific reserve needs, rapidly scalable substitutes and emergency measures with explicit expiry conditions. While essential services remain dependent on vulnerable liquid-fuel networks, resilience to oil-flow disruption should remain a core transition metric. Oil-flow resilience is a bridge out of dependence, not a rationale for prolonging it.

text:
Addressing the Barrhead Travel conference at Lake Maggiore on Saturday (3 October), Wilson said the war in Iran and the wider conflict in the Middle East, the rollout of the EU Entry-Exit System (EES) and the UK's record-breaking hot summer had conspired to subdue early demand and push business into lates.

"We did see an immediate slowing down of demand with customers across the board," Wilson said, referring to the war. "And then it moving later, and later, and later. That late demand has stuck. It's still very late."

He said that while EES and the heatwaves were inconvenient and "a pain to deal with", their effects were temporary. "This [lates demand] seems to be lagging. And when I look at the sales this week or last week, about 20% of our sales are for departures in the next 30 days, which is unheard of."

Wilson said Egypt, Cyprus, Turkey and Morocco were hardest hit by the conflict. Egypt, he said, being used to crises, reacted by "wiping the price right down". By contrast, he said Cyprus has been "a little slow" to recover, adding Turkey was turning things round.

Asked if he thought easyJet and easyJet holidays, and the wider industry, was going to pull back the late booking trend, Wilson said: "It's not good for the industry to have it so late. "I think we all collectively need to really think as the year finishes how we pull forward the sales and get turn of year back to being a really exciting time for customers."

Critical six to eight weeks

Wilson said a process of "right-sizing" capacity was imminent. "I think you'll see capacity shift, and that will be addressed in the new year. A lot of those destinations that had really good availability in July and August shouldn't really be [readily] available in July or August next year."

"Standout" destinations, he said, included Egypt and Greece, with Spain "coming back well in lates", although Wilson said he felt there was still over-capacity in Spain.

He tipped North Africa for next year. "That's where a lot of tour operator capacity will go," he continued. "And also Turkey – with Turkey, we took the capacity out very early on. We went back to 2025 levels. We'll probably put that capacity back in."

Wilson said agents had done a lot of heavy lifting for easyJet holidays during lates. "When we look at our overall sales, 20% is through high street. But when we look at lates, that's significantly higher.

"I think just having the availability, having the price, having the products they want has really helped see that market share jump up in that late market.

"We went out with the fuel promise and various other things at the beginning, but I think just sitting down in a shop with a travel agent reassuring you as a customer – [it's] really, really important. We saw customers relying on that much more through this summer."

Wilson was asked if winter and summer capacity would be dictated by oil and fuel prices and whether the current economic realities could have a negative impact on demand. "I [about it] think every day. It's hugely expensive. Of course, we had hedging, but we have to think forward. If that sticks, it becomes difficult.

"I think there will be much more focus on where you're flying, getting the sales in early, getting the load factors up, and being really careful as to whether you fly that capacity or not. I think a lot of decisions will be taken in the next six to eight weeks as to whether that flies."

Wilson said savings could end up being made elsewhere. "As an airline, your biggest cost base – 90-odd percent – is your fuel. As a tour operator, 30% of your cost base is your fuel so you have the opportunity to negotiate contracts with hotels, to negotiate with your transfer providers. You have some tools to try to offset that fuel."

'Low-level' govt interference

Elsewhere, Wilson was critical of Prime Minister Andy Burnham and recently announced government measures to crack down on some airline charges like guaranteed seating with children and extra bags. "You think, that's just going to put the price of flight tickets up," he said. "You're just going to limit the amount of people who fly.

"He [Andy Burnham] said nothing about the taxation, about APD [Air Passenger Duty], about investment in SAF [Sustainable Aviation Fuel] which is going to be hugely prohibitive if the prices goes up.

"When the government gestures on low-level things that will get soundbites to consumers, you know, that's fine if behind the scenes they're really thinking structurally about how they can support the industry. With SAF, I think they have to do a lot more, a lot quicker, which isn't happening."

Wilson narrowed in on APD. "You can't say to a customer, 'we know how important your holiday is but we're going to tax the hell out of it'. It's either important or not to them. They do need to put their money where their mouth is."

title: Air France-KLM Just Quietly Committed To Flying Its Airbus A350s & Boeing 787s Into The 2040s
description:
In Air France-KLM Group's H1 2026 report, it extended the depreciation period for its Airbus A350, Boeing 787, and A320neo family fleets from 20 to 25 years.
Simple Flying has contacted Air France-KLM for comment.
Indications Of A Substantial Long-Haul Role For Air France-KLM Recent years have seen Air France building up a significant A350 fleet.
The table below shows how Air France configures its A350-900s, making use of Simple Flying's seat map.
The order was for 21 jets to Air France and seven to KLM.
text:
In Air France-KLM Group's H1 2026 report, it extended the depreciation period for its Airbus A350, Boeing 787, and A320neo family fleets from 20 to 25 years. This accounting decision has reduced depreciation costs by €24 million in the first half alone. One interpretation of this decision is that it shows the airline group's confidence in these aircraft and their ability to operate effectively over the next couple of decades.

The group operates significant fleets of the aircraft impacted. This includes 42 A350-900s, 23 Boeing 787-9s, and 15 Boeing 787-10s. The group also has orders for 55 further A350s and six A350Fs. These fleets include Air France, HOP! (France), KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, and Transavia France, and a minority ownership of Air Calédonie, Kenya Airways, SAS Group, and WestJet Group. The size of these fleets, aircraft that are yet to arrive, and the new lengthy depreciation period suggest that the corporate group has plans for high longevity with these jets. Simple Flying has contacted Air France-KLM for comment.

What The Accounting Decision Actually Shows

It would be wrong to interpret the extension of these new planes' depreciation period as either a fixed retirement date or a firm commitment to continue flying these planes until a certain time. It is a useful indication of the time across which a carrier or airline group expects to fly a plane. However, as Fleet Wire notes, "Airlines regularly use accounting assumptions that differ from the actual date on which an aircraft leaves the fleet."

This difference can occur if an aircraft is retired early due to rising maintenance costs or the arrival of a better replacement aircraft. Alternatively, airlines may continue to fly a plane past its expected full depreciation. A reason for this could be that there have been delivery delays with a replacement aircraft. For example, the Boeing 777X delays have led some airlines to continue flying outdated Boeing 747s, 777s, Airbus A380s and more to prevent capacity shortfall. Yet, many of these jets now have extremely high operating and maintenance costs, or are considered obsolete.

The decision should also be considered as a tentative indication of the position that A350 and 787 planes will occupy within the Air France-KLM group fleets. Instead of simply replacing past widebody aircraft, these planes will likely become the foundation for the group's entire long-haul fleets, with a footprint lasting for two decades or longer.

Indications Of A Substantial Long-Haul Role For Air France-KLM

Recent years have seen Air France building up a significant A350 fleet. It has been using these jets to replace its aging Airbus A330s and Boeing 777-200ERs. This switch has been made easier because the A350 and the A330 have a common type rating. Pilots can switch between the two aircraft on a course that lasts eight days and doesn't require full simulator sessions. Carriers can use such an arrangement to enormously reduce their training expenditure.

The table below shows how Air France configures its A350-900s, making use of Simple Flying's seat map. Air France offers 292 seats on this plane. You can use these pages to understand how major airlines configure their most prevalent jets:

Likewise, KLM has spent the last several years building up a substantial Dreamliner fleet. The jet first entered the airline's fleet in 2015. Both the 787-9 and 787-10 variants have a significant role in KLM's intercontinental fleet. KLM also notes it is a preferred aircraft after its operational service, writing that "it is made of 50% composite, 20% aluminium, 15% titanium, 10% steel, and 5% other materials, generating less waste and chemicals than a similar aircraft."

Modern Aircraft Design Changes How Carriers Think About Depreciation

The cutting-edge aircraft currently emerging from the Boeing and Airbus production lines are more future-proof than ever. They use advanced composite materials, next-generation engines, and upgraded aerodynamics and flight systems. The result is greatly reduced fuel consumption and operating costs compared with older widebody aircraft. The longer that a carrier keeps such planes in service, the more cost savings they can enjoy.

An example is the A350. Airbus claims this aircraft has a 25% lower fuel burn and CO2 emissions than aircraft of the previous generation, while boasting an incredibly far 8,600 nautical miles (15,750 km) of range. For an aircraft departing from London, that's enough to reach cities like Los Angeles, Singapore and Perth. It makes use of Rolls-Royce Trent XWB engines to achieve these advances. These engines will be able to fly with a 100% blend of sustainable aviation fuel by the end of the decade.

The table below shows the specifications for the A350-900. It uses data published by Airbus:

The A350 also has an airframe constructed from 70% advanced materials. This includes 53% Carbon Fibre Reinforced Polymer (CFRP) in the fuselage, wings, and tail, alongside titanium components. CFRPs are made from carbon fibers. A polymer resin binds them together. Aluminium-lithium alloys, known for their low weight and high fatigue resistance, are also used.

The Depreciation Extension Doesn't Mean These Jets' Service Has Been Flawless

These extensions to aircraft's operational lifespan do not mean Air France-KLM expects perfect service with no operational issues. The group's carriers have already faced problems. For example, in May 2025, Simple Flying's Alexander Mitchell reported that maintenance concerns had forced a grounding of seven of KLM's Dreamliners. The airline reported that maintenance procedures related to a refueling system had not been followed. The grounding led to flight cancelations and delays for several hundred passengers.

"Although there is no safety risk, the seven aircraft will remain grounded and undergo expedited maintenance," said the airline in an NL Times-published statement. It said that the repairs would begin "as quickly as possible." The flights impacted included services from KLM's Amsterdam Schiphol Airport (AMS) hub to Mexico City International Airport (MEX), Chicago-O'Hare International Airport (ORD), and Portland International Airport (PDX).

The table below shows the state of KLM's 787 fleet when the groundings occurred:

The fuel system in question utilized the same parts as KLM's Boeing 777 fleet. However, there are differences in the maintenance procedures needed to keep these jets in the skies. This shared system both explains how the problem might have initially arisen and made it easier for KLM to amend the issues.

How The A350 Ended Up In The Air France Fleet

Considerations of the roles that these aircraft will have for Air France-KLM in the years to come require some attention to how they ended up in these airlines' fleets and the initial roles that they were expected to have. In June 2013, Air France-KLM placed its first A350 order. The order was for 21 jets to Air France and seven to KLM. The decision changed in 2020, with Air France set to exclusively operate the A350 and KLM only use the Dreamliner out of the two jets. Simplifying their fleets created more commonality, reducing the costs of training and maintenance.

The first A350 arrived in Air France's fleet on September 27, 2019. The carrier named this jet 'Toulouse' after the city that is home to the Airbus assembly line. It has continued to name each further A350 that has arrived after a different location in France.

The table below uses Planespotters.net data to show the registration, name, and delivery date for Air France's ten oldest A350s. It shows the huge distance that these jets remain away from their full depreciation under the new 25-year plan:

Air France-KLM made a further order for A350 jets, responding to the success that the plane had experienced in the Air France fleet. The order included 50 firm commitments with options for 40 more jets. At the time, the completed order would have made the group the largest operator of the A350. It now uses the jet to fly some mammoth routes. Its longest one-stop route is from CDG to Papeete via Los Angeles. This route has a block time of 22 hours and 20 minutes, and makes use of Air France's fifth freedom flights between Los Angeles and Tahiti. The frequency ranges from five weekly to daily and uses the A350-900 exclusively.

title: The expansion of Heathrow would be an expensive disaster for Britain and the world ...
description:
For decades, government ministers have told us that airport expansion is essential for “growth”.
Though Heathrow expansion remains official policy, when asked at the weekend, Andy Burnham said the runway was “contested” and “principally it’s a matter for London and London MPs”.
Successive governments have justified airport expansion plans with the promise of “sustainable aviation fuel”.
If Heathrow expansion goes ahead, passenger numbers in the UK are forecast to rise from 299 million in 2025 to 491 million in 2050.
What government support for airport expansion shows is that “growth” is simply an excuse for giving powerful lobby groups what they want.
text:
If a third runway is built at Heathrow, what will be the impact on the wealth of the nation? It will cost us somewhere between £23.4bn and £62.5bn. These are not my figures; they weren’t calculated by environmental groups, but by the Department for Transport.

For decades, government ministers have told us that airport expansion is essential for “growth”. As chancellor, Rachel Reeves claimed that a third runway at Heathrow would add 0.43% to GDP, figures we later discovered came from a report commissioned by the airport. The transport department’s own analysis concluded that the real addition to GDP would be between 0.03% and 0.05%: eight to 14 times less. Against this, it weighed the social and environmental costs of the project, to reveal a massive net loss. It found that a third runway would cause major harm to the health and wellbeing of up to 3 million local people.

But even these figures don’t capture it. The climate breakdown caused by the runway affects the entire planet, yet the costs to other countries aren’t counted. So again we must ask, why does the government support it?

Or does it? Though Heathrow expansion remains official policy, when asked at the weekend, Andy Burnham said the runway was “contested” and “principally it’s a matter for London and London MPs”. That sounds hopeful.

We also learned that the project has been delayed yet again. Though Heathrow announced last year that its plans were “shovel-ready”, it now admits the runway would take four years longer to build than it claimed: the estimated completion date is now 2039.

By then, or so we must hope, a government might have decided to take the climate impact seriously. If so, the new runway would need to be shuttered the moment it opened. Otherwise, according to the government’s Climate Change Committee, “almost all CO2 emissions in 2050 will be from aviation”. Heathrow’s expansion alone, the committee says, would cause more carbon emissions by 2054 than “any other sector of the economy”.

And even this is not the end of it. The committee considers only the carbon dioxide planes produce, but the other impacts are even greater. A paper in the journal Atmospheric Environment suggests that, over 100 years, the nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, soot, volatile organic products, water vapour and other compounds released or formed in the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere by planes raise the heating caused by flying by 115%. Over 20 years, they raise it by an astonishing 517%.

Given that crucial Earth systems may be approaching their tipping points, and heating today triggers further greenhouse gas releases from forests, wetlands and permafrost, the 20-year horizon is crucial. But these other compounds are considered in neither international treaties nor the UK’s Climate Change Act. The impact of flying is officially and massively underestimated.

While the heating effects of almost all other sectors can be greatly reduced by technology, there are simply no good solutions for aviation. Successive governments have justified airport expansion plans with the promise of “sustainable aviation fuel”. Mostly they mean turning biomass into kerosene, which is even worse than using fossil fuels. If this substitute is to reach any kind of scale, it will either swallow up existing cropland, driving starvation, or it will cause the expansion of cropland into forests, wetlands and other habitats, accelerating the environmental crisis. An analysis by the Royal Society found that meeting existing UK aviation demand (never mind future growth) with energy crops “would require around half of UK agricultural land”. That’s the opposite of sustainable.

“Sustainable aviation fuel” can also mean synthetic fuels made from captured CO2 and green hydrogen. But the Royal Society found that for existing aviation, we’d need to use between five and eight times the UK’s entire renewable electricity capacity. And still, aeroplanes would release a lethal chemical cocktail – not just CO2 but those other compounds – into the high atmosphere, so only a fraction of the problem would be solved. Worldwide, a paper in the journal One Earth found that even with a wildly unrealistic programme of technological change, in which fossil jet fuels were phased out completely by 2040, the global heating caused by aviation would more than double by 2070, thanks to rising demand.

As for hydrogen-, ammonia- or battery-powered commercial aircraft, they all fail on technical or safety grounds, even before we ask where the power comes from. The “prototypes” endlessly showcased by the airlines, which never get beyond the artist’s impression, are nothing but “perceptionware”, designed to solve political problems, not technical ones.

If Heathrow expansion goes ahead, passenger numbers in the UK are forecast to rise from 299 million in 2025 to 491 million in 2050. As other sectors decarbonise, the proportion of climate breakdown caused by flying climbs and climbs, until planes account for almost all of it.

The only effective strategy is to reduce demand. There’s a progressive means of doing so: the frequent flyer levy. Wealth and flights are strongly linked. In 2024, 48% of England’s population did not fly at all. But 5% of the population took five or more flights abroad, and these account for 33% of all journeys. Increasing demand has been almost entirely driven by frequent flyers, who are highly concentrated in the highest income quintile. The levy would not be charged on the first flight someone took in any year, but it would escalate with every additional flight.

This is just, proportionate and – unlike all the techno-bollocks – immediately dispatchable. Otherwise, we continue to subsidise a wealthy, selfish minority with our money, our health, our wellbeing and the degradation of the living planet. How is that fair?

What government support for airport expansion shows is that “growth” is simply an excuse for giving powerful lobby groups what they want. When asked whether growth was more important than net zero, Reeves replied: “Well, if it’s the No 1 mission, it’s obviously the most important thing.” That’s another way of saying money is more important than human life. But, as the figures show, it was never about growth at all. It was always about meeting the demands of the airport lobby and wealthy passengers.

Now we wait on Burnham. Will the flight of reason continue? Or will human and planetary welfare at last outweigh the lobbyists?

Media Release 12 March 2026 - Sydney Airport

Australians Back Locally Produced Sustainable Aviation Fuel and Regional Jobs

New research commissioned by Sydney Airport shows strong public support for building a domestic Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) industry, with Australians recognising the opportunity to create regional jobs, support farmers and keep more of Australia’s natural resources and manufacturing capability at home.

Australia already produces many of the feedstocks needed to make SAF - from agricultural crops and residues to used cooking oil and household waste, yet much of this material is currently exported overseas to be processed into fuel.

Sydney Airport CEO Scott Charlton said Australia has a significant opportunity to develop a new regional industry centred on Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF).

“Locally producing SAF would reduce aviation emissions while creating jobs, supporting farmers, and strengthening Australia’s fuel security, and we continue to advocate for demand measures as part of the Australian Government’s $1.1 billion investment in low-carbon liquid fuels.

“The current conflict in the Middle East highlights the importance of mandates that attract global investment and secure a domestic fuel supply. Globally, SAF mandates are accelerating, and Australia must implement measures to boost domestic SAF production, using feedstock that would otherwise be exported.”

Public support for sustainable aviation fuel is also stronger than many people realise. Research conducted by Sydney Airport in early March, revealed that although awareness of SAF remains relatively low, especially among those who hadn’t flown in the past year, support rises to 60 percent of Australians once they understand what SAF is and how it functions.

Nearly 70 percent of Australians said they support the use of sustainable aviation fuel, and the majority said they would be willing to contribute small amounts through airline tickets to help accelerate its development.

There is also a clear preference for Australian-made fuel.

The strongest motivator for a domestic SAF industry is reducing aircraft emissions (57 percent), but Australians also recognise the value of:

using renewable Australian resources (49 percent)

climate and broader environmental benefits (48 percent)

improved fuel security (45 percent)

supporting Australian manufacturing (43 percent)

job creation and economic growth (42 percent)

Support was higher among frequent flyers and business travellers. Environmental concern was also a contributing factor, with 48 percent of Australians reporting concerns about the environmental impact of aircraft fuel emissions.

The research also revealed a strong expectation for enhanced information and transparency, with respondents expressing greater confidence in SAF when given clear, fact-based explanations of its production process, the application of safety standards, and the methods used to achieve emissions reductions.

“Australians want to see this industry built here because they recognise the benefits for farmers, regional communities and Australia’s long-term fuel security,” Sydney Airport CEO Scott Charlton said.

“With global aviation demand continuing to grow, the window to establish a domestic Sustainable Aviation Fuel industry is now.

“Building fuel infrastructure takes time - often close to a decade from investment decision to production - so the opportunity is to start building that capability now and supporting regional economies.”

Sydney Airport is participating in the Bioenergy Australia Renewable Fuels Summit in Sydney this week, which brings together government, industry and investors to examine the role of renewable and low carbon liquid fuels in supporting emissions reduction, fuel security and domestic manufacturing.

The report surveyed Australians on their views on SAF, including affordability considerations, domestic production and fuel security.

The research was conducted in early March 2026, prior to the conflict in the Middle East.

MEDIA RELEASE - 12 March 2026

New APAC benchmark report highlights renewable fuels opportunity to

strengthen Australia’s fuel security

A new Asia-Pacific benchmark report has found Australia has the resources and policy foundations to build a major renewable fuels industry, but risks falling behind regional competitors unless investment and market demand accelerate.

The Low Carbon Fuels Alliance of Australia and New Zealand (LCFAANZ) - an industry alliance established by Bioenergy Australia to accelerate low-carbon fuel development - released the APAC Low Carbon Fuels Benchmark Report today at the Renewable Fuels Summit,, assessing how 19 economies across the region are positioning themselves to produce fuels such as sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel and renewable gas.

The report comes amid growing global concern about fuel security, with Australia currently relying heavily on imported liquid fuels, exposed to supply disruptions and rising global energy prices.

Bioenergy Australia CEO Shahana McKenzie said the benchmark highlights both the opportunity and urgency for Australia to develop domestic renewable fuel production, “Australia imports the majority of its liquid fuels, which leaves our economy exposed to global supply disruptions and price volatility,”

“Renewable fuels produced from Australian feedstocks provide a practical pathway to strengthen fuel security while reducing emissions in sectors like aviation, shipping and heavy transport that are difficult to electrify.” McKenzie said.

Industry analysis suggests Australia has sufficient feedstock resources to underpin a renewable fuels industry worth more than $10 billion annually, supporting more than 26,000 jobs, many of them in regional areas.

The benchmark compares countries across four key indicators: government policy ambition, feedstock availability, fuel production capacity and carbon accounting maturity.

It finds Australia sits within a group of “constrained leader” economies, alongside countries such as Japan, Korea, China and Singapore. These economies show strong policy intent and favourable conditions for industry development but have yet to establish large-scale production capacity.

In contrast, countries including Indonesia, Malaysia and Thailand were identified as “high potential leaders”, with strong feedstock resources, clear policy frameworks and emerging project pipelines supporting renewable fuel production.

The report also highlights a growing shift in global fuel markets, with governments increasingly using blending mandates and demand-side policies to drive investment in sustainable fuels.

Across Asia-Pacific, aviation fuel mandates are gaining momentum. Singapore will require 1 per cent sustainable aviation fuel on departing flights, while South Korea will introduce a mandate from 2027 and Thailand has already introduced blending requirements.

Australia currently has no national sustainable aviation fuel mandate, although voluntary airline targets and some state-based policies are emerging.

The report also warns that biomass and waste oils are rapidly becoming strategic resources, with governments moving to secure domestic feedstocks as demand for renewable fuels accelerates.

Recent policy moves in Asia include export restrictions and supply controls on key feedstocks such as used cooking oil, highlighting growing competition for the raw materials needed to produce renewable fuels.

Australia has significant feedstock advantages, including agricultural residues, waste oils, municipal waste and biomass resources. However, the report notes that a substantial share of these feedstocks is currently exported, which could limit domestic fuel production if policy settings do not encourage local processing.

McKenzie said the benchmark shows renewable fuels represent a major opportunity for Australia to strengthen energy resilience while supporting regional industries, “With abundant feedstocks, strong research capability and growing investor interest, Australia has the ingredients to become a regional producer of renewable fuels,”

“The question now is whether we move quickly enough to convert those advantages into domestic production and investment.” concluded McKenzie.

text:
NorSAF and Nova Pangaea have entered into a partnership aimed at addressing Europe’s growing sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) demand while developing more resilient, locally sourced feedstock supply chains, Hydrocarbon Engineering reported.

SAF production in Europe is expected to expand significantly over the coming decade. Under EU regulations, aviation fuel suppliers must increase the share of SAF supplied at EU airports from 2% in 2025 to 6% in 2030 and 20% by 2035.

Although Europe produces a significant share of its current SAF domestically, the sector relies heavily on Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) technology. Meeting the regulated targets through this pathway requires large quantities of feedstocks such as used cooking oil.

Around 85% of Europe’s SAF feedstocks are currently sourced from overseas, with China accounting for 61% of the supply.

While existing production capacity is technically expected to support Europe’s near-term 2030 targets, continued dependence on imported feedstocks, including Chinese used cooking oil, could create supply chain security risks as SAF demand increases.

Agricultural and forestry residues could provide regional alternatives, particularly in countries such as Latvia, where these biomass resources are available. The partners said advanced SAF plants such as NorSAF could help utilise these resources to produce aviation fuel from alternative local feedstocks.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA® technology converts waste biomass, including woody and agricultural residues, into ethanol and biochar. The biochar acts as a co-product that permanently captures carbon, making the overall process carbon negative.

The locally produced ethanol can subsequently be converted into SAF through the alcohol-to-jet pathway as part of NorSAF’s planned SAF production.

Janis Kisiels, founder and Board Member of NorSAF, said Europe’s energy security would require not only reducing fossil-fuel imports but also developing domestic industrial capacity to produce the clean fuels that will replace them.

He said Europe’s dependence on overseas feedstocks such as used cooking oil leaves the aviation sector exposed to international supply chain disruptions. According to Kisiels, using waste resources available in Europe, particularly in the Baltic region, could help establish a domestic and resilient SAF supply chain.

“Our partnership with Nova Pangaea is a crucial milestone in developing that strategic capability right here in Latvia, ensuring our future SAF production is sustainable, secure, and locally anchored,” he said.

Jonathan Wood, Chief Commercial Officer of Nova Pangaea, said the partnership would provide NorSAF’s SAF project with carbon-negative ethanol produced from locally sourced biomass waste.

He described the collaboration as a model for partnerships needed to expand SAF production in Europe and other regions by strengthening energy security, creating domestic industries, generating jobs and economic growth, and reducing fossil-fuel emissions.

Wood cited International Air Transport Association (IATA) estimates that Europe has sufficient waste biomass resources to produce enough SAF to meet its ambitious 2050 targets.
