Each Friday, we publish a round-up of the 20 most important stories on sustainable aviation. You can see previous editions of #Sustainability20 here.

Industry, policy and carbon markets

Canada’s SAF industry faces $32B GDP opportunity as energy security joins climate goals - AviNews

A new analysis estimates that developing Canada’s SAF industry could create a $32 billion GDP opportunity between 2026 and 2040. It presents domestic SAF production as both a decarbonisation opportunity and an energy-security strategy, linking the sector to Canadian feedstocks, jobs and reduced exposure to international fuel-price volatility.

FlyORO joins the ICAO finvest hub as a partner, bringing modular SAF blending expertise to aviation decarbonisation finance - FlyORO

FlyORO has joined ICAO’s Finvest Hub as a partner, contributing modular SAF-blending expertise to the platform’s work on financing aviation-decarbonisation projects. The partnership is aimed at helping projects address the practical infrastructure and financing barriers involved in SAF deployment.

IBA forecasts 87% rise in gross aviation emissions by 2050 despite efficiency gains - GreenAir News

IBA forecasts that global aviation’s gross CO2 emissions could rise by 87% between 2025 and 2050, despite a projected 20% improvement in fleet fuel efficiency. Passenger growth is expected to outpace those efficiency gains, reinforcing the need for measures beyond aircraft efficiency alone.

SimpliFlying’s Carbon Removal Diaries: What really goes into choosing a carbon credit?

After measuring our team’s business travel emissions this summer, we are now examining how to respond to them. This third instalment of our Carbon Removal Diaries explains the questions we asked when evaluating carbon credits, including what a credit represents, how projects are assessed, and what buyers should consider before making a claim.

Sustainable aviation fuels (SAF)

Plug and Arcadia eFuels sign strategic partnership covering more than 1 GW of e-SAF projects, starting with 280 MW to turn danish renewable electricity into jet fuel - GlobeNewswire

Plug Power and Arcadia eFuels have announced a strategic partnership covering more than 1 GW of potential e-SAF projects. The initial 280 MW Danish project is planned to use renewable electricity to produce hydrogen, which would then be combined with captured carbon to make synthetic aviation fuel.

Aether Fuels successfully demonstrates 2.5 barrel-per-day Aurora™ equipment in fully integrated line producing on-spec synthetic aviation fuel - GlobeNewswire

Aether Fuels has demonstrated a fully integrated line producing 2.5 barrels per day of synthetic aviation fuel. The process uses renewable natural gas derived from landfill gas and captured industrial CO2; the company reports that independent testing confirmed the fuel met the FT-SPK specification under ASTM D7566.

ARC Bio demonstrates Canadian forest residue pathway to sustainable aviation fuel - ARC Bio

ARC Bio, a Canadian joint venture between Bioénergie AE Côte-Nord and Alder Renewables, has demonstrated a pilot-scale refinery co-processing pathway for converting forest-industry residues into lower-carbon jet fuel. The approach is intended to use existing refinery infrastructure, although the demonstration does not by itself establish commercial-scale production.

Business, forestry and agriculture leaders unite to advance sustainable aviation fuels - PR Newswire

Agriculture, forestry and business organisations in Georgia, US, have formed a new SAF coalition. Founding members include the Metro Atlanta Chamber, Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines, working to accelerate domestic biofuel production using Georgia-grown agricultural and forestry feedstocks.

KLM and KLM Cityhopper raise awareness of SAF during The Aviation Challenge - KLM

As part of SkyTeam’s Aviation Challenge, KLM operated a showcase flight from Amsterdam to Delhi on September 28, while KLM Cityhopper flew from Amsterdam to Dublin on September 30 using an Embraer E195-E2. Both flights will test initiatives aimed at improving operational efficiency, reducing fuel consumption and increasing awareness of SAF.

Infrastructure and operational efficiencies

IAG selects SkyBreathe to support fuel efficiency across its airlines - OpenAirlines

IAG will deploy OpenAirlines’ SkyBreathe platform across Aer Lingus, British Airways, Iberia, LEVEL and Vueling, covering more than 600 aircraft. By analysing flight plans, weather and aircraft-performance data, the platform will help identify fuel-saving opportunities and create a common framework for measuring and sharing efficiency initiatives across the group.

Noi Bai International Airport achieves Level 1 Airport Carbon Accreditation - ACI Asia-Pacific

Noi Bai International Airport has achieved Level 1 Airport Carbon Accreditation, becoming the first airport in Vietnam to join the programme. The certification establishes an emissions baseline and provides a foundation for future carbon-reduction measures.

Bristol Airport funds three new projects to cut aviation emissions - ADS Advance

Bristol Airport is funding three technology projects exploring wind power, carbon capture and hydrogen-electric aircraft operations through its 2026 Aviation Carbon Transition Programme. The programme received a record 28 applications and provides up to £150,000 in total funding for projects addressing aviation and airport-related emissions, particularly Scope 3 emissions.

Pittsburgh International Airport deploys robot dogs powered by AI for safety and efficiency - Aerospace Global News

Pittsburgh International Airport is preparing to trial up to four quadruped robots with Pittsburgh-based Skild AI. Initially, they will collect indoor air-quality data and spot issues such as spills and overflowing bins, with later tests covering crowd monitoring, biological-threat detection and terminal deliveries.

New aerodynamic testing technique could improve aircraft efficiency - Aerospace Global News

Pressure-sensitive paint is being used in wind-tunnel testing to capture detailed airflow and surface-pressure data. The technique could help aircraft designers improve aerodynamic efficiency and reduce fuel burn.

Aviation cyber attacks cost organisations $1.4m on average, as phishing and threats to airport operational systems raise concerns - Aerospace Global News

A survey of aviation organisations found that cyber breaches cost an average of $1.4 million. Phishing and attacks on airport operational systems are raising concerns as airports and airlines become increasingly dependent on connected infrastructure.

New technology: Electric and hydrogen

Abu Dhabi plans Emirate-wide air taxi network with over 10 vertiports, targeting late 2026 or early 2027 launch - AviNews

Abu Dhabi is developing an emirate-wide air taxi network with more than 10 vertiports and is targeting passenger operations by late 2026 or early 2027. Archer is expected to supply its Midnight eVTOL aircraft, while Abu Dhabi Aviation will operate the initial service.

Nimbus Aerospace tests quarter-scale prototype in Oregon as hybrid-electric race ramps up - GeekWire

Nimbus Aerospace has conducted test flights of a quarter-scale NX1 prototype in Oregon. The company is developing a proposed six- to eight-seat hybrid-electric aircraft.

Pilotless plane flies over Wichita, putting the future of aviation on display - Yahoo News

Joby Aviation demonstrated an autonomous aircraft over Wichita using a Cessna Caravan retrofitted with its technology. The aircraft used cameras, radar and other sensors to manage flight functions, while a person onboard monitored the demonstration.

Vertical Aerospace opens Valo assembly centre with 1,000 aircraft a year in its sights - Aerospace Global News

Vertical Aerospace has opened its Aircraft Assembly Centre at Cotswold Airport, converting a former Second World War-era and Red Arrows hangar into a production facility for its Valo electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft. The first certification-conforming aircraft is scheduled to begin assembly in late 2027, with first flight planned for 2028.

Deutsche Aircraft opens D328eco® final assembly line in Leipzig - Deutsche Aircraft

Deutsche Aircraft has inaugurated the D328eco Final Assembly Line at Leipzig/Halle Airport, marking the programme’s transition from development to serial production. The opening establishes Leipzig as the production site for Germany’s next-generation regional aircraft and marks the return of aircraft manufacturing to Saxony after more than 60 years.

EHang expands global fast-track programme to Vietnam - eVTOL Insights

EHang has expanded its Global Fast Track Program to Vietnam, working with Hanoi’s Department of Science and Technology and local partner HungViet to establish a regulatory sandbox for pilotless eVTOL aircraft. Subject to approval, controlled EH216-S test flights at Hoa Lac Hi-Tech Park will explore unmanned-aircraft traffic management and operations-control systems.

text:
ATLANTA — Agricultural, forestry and business leaders in Georgia have banded together to launch the Georgia Sustainable Aviation Fuel Coalition.

The goal is to advance research and the state’s production of biofuels, according to an announcement Wednesday.

The coalition was established by multiple organizations and businesses, including the Metro Atlanta Chamber, the Georgia Farm Bureau, the Georgia Forestry Association and Delta Air Lines.

Sustainable aviation fuel is processed from agricultural and forestry feedstocks to reduce air travel emissions and is designed for compatibility with existing aircraft and fueling infrastructure. Although biofuel currently represents a small share of global aviation fuel, demand is expanding across global markets.

The coalition’s formation builds on the Keep Georgia Forested Act, which Gov. Brian Kemp signed into law in May 2026.

The legislation allows companies to transfer certain tax credits during early construction and operational stages, supporting forestry manufacturing and biofuel production facilities.

Business leaders highlighted the initiative as an opportunity to integrate regional supply chains with aviation demand.

Katie Kirkpatrick, president and CEO of the Metro Atlanta Chamber, outlined the coalition’s goal of coordinating statewide stakeholders.

“This is about aligning Georgia’s natural strengths with real market demand,” Kirkpatrick said.

Agricultural producers said they expect the initiative to expand commercial opportunities for local commodities and the initiative’s connection to Georgia’s farming industry.

The state’s forestry sector, which includes 22 million acres of working forests, is slated to supply additional raw materials for fuel processing.

Prior to the formal launch, coalition members joined the Georgia Research Alliance to secure state funding for an Eminent Scholar focused on forestry research and biofuel development.

Aviation and corporate partners have also signed on to support the project. Boeing, Cox Enterprises and Norfolk Southern are serving as anchor partners, with additional backing from supporting partners RYAM and Gulfstream Aerospace.

Peter Carter, president of Delta Air Lines, pointed to the state’s positioning in the sector as a positive for the new coalition.

“Georgia is well positioned to become a national leader in SAF,” Carter said. “The Georgia SAF Coalition unites organizations committed to advancing that opportunity. Together, we can power the growth of a SAF industry that strengthens Georgia’s economy, supports innovation and creates lasting benefits for communities across the state.”

Federal agriculture officials expressed support for the state-level public-private initiative as well.

The coalition said its immediate priorities include bringing sustainable aviation fuel and biofuel facilities to Georgia, linking university research with industry needs and establishing a supply chain to connect local farms and forests directly to aviation markets.

title: How UCO-Based Biofuels Are Reshaping Aviation and Maritime in the MENA Region
description:
The SAF Opportunity Sustainable Aviation Fuel is chemically similar to conventional jet fuel but produced from renewable feedstocks, including UCO.
The UAE has signalled its commitment through the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Roadmap 2030, which outlines the nation's plan to integrate SAF into its aviation sector.
Maritime Biofuels: Fujairah's Emerging Role Fujairah, already the world's third-largest marine fuelling centre, is positioning itself as a hub for biofuel bunkering.
Why UCO Is the Preferred Feedstock UCO-derived biofuels hold a particular advantage in both aviation and maritime applications.
Every litre of UCO we collect today has the potential to serve road transport, maritime, or aviation applications — depending on market needs and processing pathways.
text:
A New Frontier for Waste-Derived Fuels

When most people think of biodiesel, they picture trucks and buses running on cleaner fuel. But the next chapter of the biofuel story is being written in the skies and on the seas — and the MENA region is emerging as a key player.

Used cooking oil (UCO), the same feedstock that powers road-going biodiesel, is now at the centre of the global push toward Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) and cleaner marine fuels. For the UAE and its neighbours, this represents a convergence of environmental ambition, strategic geography, and existing waste-to-fuel infrastructure.

The SAF Opportunity

Sustainable Aviation Fuel is chemically similar to conventional jet fuel but produced from renewable feedstocks, including UCO. When derived from waste oils, SAF can reduce lifecycle carbon emissions by up to 80% compared to fossil jet fuel — without requiring any modifications to aircraft or airport fuelling infrastructure.

The UAE has signalled its commitment through the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Roadmap 2030, which outlines the nation's plan to integrate SAF into its aviation sector. Given that Dubai International Airport is one of the world's busiest aviation hubs and Abu Dhabi continues to expand its aviation footprint, the domestic demand for SAF is substantial and growing.

Notably, MENA Biofuels, a subsidiary of Dubai-headquartered Mercantile and Maritime Group, is currently developing what it describes as the UAE's first commercial SAF production facility in Fujairah. The facility is part of a broader strategy that includes securing sustainable feedstock through international partnerships, such as a recent MoU with Indonesia's Ministry of Cooperatives to develop a nationwide UCO collection ecosystem.

This cross-border collaboration highlights a critical reality: the SAF industry will require feedstock volumes that exceed what any single country can supply domestically, making international UCO supply chains essential.

Maritime Biofuels: Fujairah's Emerging Role

Fujairah, already the world's third-largest marine fuelling centre, is positioning itself as a hub for biofuel bunkering. The maritime sector faces increasing pressure from the EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation, which mandates progressive reductions in greenhouse gas emissions from shipping fuels starting with a 2% reduction against the 2020 baseline.

B24 blends — consisting of 24% UCO methyl ester (UCOME) mixed with very low sulphur fuel oil (VLSFO) — have already entered the Fujairah market, though supply constraints and sporadic demand have limited uptake so far. Industry participants expect demand to accelerate as shipowners prepare for more stringent IMO and EU mandates in the coming years.

The partnership between Uniper Energy Dubai and Neutral Fuels to deliver maritime biofuel in Fujairah is one example of how UAE-based producers are connecting local UCO-to-biodiesel capability with the maritime sector's decarbonisation needs.

Why UCO Is the Preferred Feedstock

UCO-derived biofuels hold a particular advantage in both aviation and maritime applications. Because the feedstock is 100% waste — no virgin crops are used — it avoids the sustainability controversies associated with palm oil or soy-based biofuels. Under EU regulations, waste-derived biofuels receive favourable treatment in emissions accounting and are not subject to the crop-based feedstock caps that limit other biofuel types.

For ISCC-certified producers like Neutral Fuels, this means UCO-derived biodiesel and its derivatives are well-positioned to meet the traceability and sustainability requirements of international markets, including export destinations in Europe.

The MENA Advantage

The MENA region has several structural advantages in the emerging biofuel supply chain. The UAE and GCC states host some of the world's highest per-capita food service activity, generating significant volumes of UCO. Strategic locations like Fujairah provide direct access to major shipping lanes. And established refining infrastructure can be adapted for biofuel production.

Saudi Arabia, through its Vision 2030 programme, has also begun exploring biofuel integration as part of its energy diversification strategy. As cross-border feedstock agreements develop and regulatory frameworks mature, the potential for a MENA-wide biofuel ecosystem becomes increasingly tangible.

What This Means for Neutral Fuels

Neutral Fuels' 14-plus years of UCO collection and biodiesel production experience positions us at the foundation of this expanding value chain. Every litre of UCO we collect today has the potential to serve road transport, maritime, or aviation applications — depending on market needs and processing pathways.

As SAF and marine biofuel demand scales up across the region, the importance of robust, certified UCO collection networks will only grow. For businesses generating used cooking oil, this means your waste stream is becoming more valuable — and more strategically important — than ever before.

text:
Los Angeles World Airports (LAWA) has presented Clay Lacy Aviation with two awards recognising its efforts at Van Nuys Airport (VNY): the VNY Friendly Flyer Award, which the company has now received 10 times, and an inaugural VNY Green Tenant Award.

The Friendly Flyer Award recognises jet operators that demonstrate “exceptional compliance” with voluntary aircraft noise abatement procedures at VNY, going beyond mandatory requirements to reduce noise impacts on surrounding communities. Criteria include increasing southbound jet departures, avoiding overnight flights, and achieving 99% or greater compliance with the No Early Turn and Quiet Jet Departure programmes.

The new Green Tenant Program recognises VNY tenants “demonstrating environmental leadership and sustainable best practices”. Clay Lacy was cited specifically for its advancements in zero-emission ground support equipment.

“Clay Lacy continues to set a benchmark for what it means to be an exceptional neighbour and partner at Van Nuys Airport,” said Jacob Haik, airport manager at Van Nuys Airport. “Earning the Fly Friendly Award reflects their ongoing diligence in adhering to our mandatory and voluntary noise abatement procedures, while their recognition as an inaugural Green Tenant Awardee demonstrates real leadership in sustainable aviation. Meaningful progress happens when airport operators proactively invest in the well-being of our local community and the future of our environment, and Clay Lacy’s efforts reflect that shared commitment.”

“Being a good neighbour to our communities has always been important to us,” said Scott Cutshall, president of real estate and sustainability at Clay Lacy Aviation. “These recognitions reflect the intentional work of our team to reduce noise, lower emissions and continually look for practical ways to thoughtfully implement sustainability strategies into all aspects of operations and facilities.”

Across its wider network, Clay Lacy’s sustainability practices include the use of electric ground equipment, renewable electricity sourcing, electric vehicle charging infrastructure, recycling programmes and the availability of Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF). The company’s facilities have held carbon-neutral certification since 2019.

The awards were presented on 23 September 2026 at Van Nuys City Hall during a recognition breakfast and ceremony hosted by LAWA.

title: Air France-KLM welcomes KLM's first Airbus A350 aircraft
description:
On October 2, 2026, KLM took delivery of its first Airbus A350-900 aircraft.
This inaugural delivery follows successive orders placed by Air France-KLM resulting in an order book of 99 Airbus A350 aircraft for both the passenger and freighter version of the aircraft, with purchase rights for an additional 40 aircraft.
This places Air France-KLM as one of the world’s largest A350 family aircraft operators.
“Today is an important milestone for KLM and the Group, with both of our network carriers now operating Airbus A350 aircraft”, said Benjamin Smith, CEO of Air France-KLM.
As of October 2, 2026, Air France-KLM operated a fleet of 593 aircraft to over 320 destinations worldwide.
text:
On October 2, 2026, KLM took delivery of its first Airbus A350-900 aircraft. The aircraft is fitted with 331 seats in a three-class configuration: 34 in World Business Class, 26 in Premium Comfort, and 271 in Economy. It will operate its first commercial flight out of Amsterdam Schiphol Airport to Toronto Pearson Airport in the coming weeks. Other destinations of the first A350 during the IATA Winter 2026 flight season will include Montreal, Kilimanjaro, Dar es Salaam, Nairobi, and Zanzibar.

With this milestone, KLM joins Air France in the list of A350 operators. Air France took delivery of its first A350 in 2019 and currently operates 43 aircraft of the type.

This inaugural delivery follows successive orders placed by Air France-KLM resulting in an order book of 99 Airbus A350 aircraft for both the passenger and freighter version of the aircraft, with purchase rights for an additional 40 aircraft. This places Air France-KLM as one of the world’s largest A350 family aircraft operators.

“Today is an important milestone for KLM and the Group, with both of our network carriers now operating Airbus A350 aircraft”, said Benjamin Smith, CEO of Air France-KLM. “By introducing the A350, KLM is taking the next step in bringing quieter, more fuel-efficient aircraft into its long-haul fleet. Our massive investment highlights our sincere commitment to the Netherlands, to Dutch connectivity, and to building a stronger KLM for the future.”

KLM expects to receive a second A350-900 aircraft this year, and deliveries will steadily continue in the coming years. To name the A350s in its fleet, KLM has chosen well-known Dutch works of art. The first A350 will carry the name The Night Watch by Rembrandt van Rijn, which is perhaps the Netherlands’ best-known masterpiece, attracting visitors from around the world to the Rijksmuseum. The second aircraft will be named Girl with a Pearl Earring.

Benefiting from the latest technological innovations, the Airbus A350 offers the best performance in its category for the network needs of the Group’s airlines. Compared to previous generation aircraft, it offers a 40% noise reduction as well as a 25% reduction in fuel consumption.

Fleet renewal is the first lever to cut CO2 and noise emissions, with immediate effect. Alongside the use of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF), operational measures such as eco-piloting, and offering intermodal travel options to our customers via our Air+Rail offering, it is one of the pillars of the Group's decarbonization trajectory.

By 2030, Air France-KLM’s goal is to reach an up to 80% share of new generation aircraft in the Group’s fleet, compared to 38% as of July 2026.

As of October 2, 2026, Air France-KLM operated a fleet of 593 aircraft to over 320 destinations worldwide.

title: Aviation Fuel Spotlight: Oil is flowing, but Jet A didn't get the memo - Globalair.com
description:
Not this month... 2026 has yielded several unprecedented peaks in retail jet fuel prices, and September's FBO reports to GlobalAir.com only raised that ceiling.
Jet A's September national average finalized at $7.99, though it's worth noting that its live national average at the time of writing is well over $8.00.
Gulf Coast wholesale jet fuel topped out the same day at $4.705 per gallon, its highest price since April 2022.
We are entering October with a live national average of $8.26 at the time of writing, well above September's average Jet A price.

text:
Usually, a new record is something to celebrate. Not this month... 2026 has yielded several unprecedented peaks in retail jet fuel prices, and September's FBO reports to GlobalAir.com only raised that ceiling. Jet A's September national average finalized at $7.99, though it's worth noting that its live national average at the time of writing is well over $8.00.

Not to be overshadowed, 100LL's September average landed at $7.59, officially setting its own high score for monthly averages. We're breaking records like a broken record now.

Tensions in the Middle East continued to fester throughout September. Houthi forces took Perim Island and most of Yemen's Red Sea coast, tightening their grip on Bab al-Mandeb, though Windward continues to track ships traversing the strait. A drone attack that Saudi and Iraqi officials say was launched from Iraq shut down the East-West pipeline, the main bypass used to avoid Hormuz. Though back online, the pipeline has not returned to pre-attack volume.

According to Reuters, oil is also moving through Hormuz itself, much of it aboard tankers with deactivated transponders. Kpler estimates shipments through Hormuz and the routes that bypass it reached nearly 80 percent of prewar levels in late September. However, refined products are a different story. Kpler puts refined flow through the strait at less than one-fifth of its prewar pace. On Sept. 26, President Donald Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.

Brent crude spot and futures prices typically sit within a few dollars of each other. On Sept. 15, Brent spot reached $130.80 while Brent futures settled at $108.75. That is a roughly $22 gap that points to tight physical supply.

Gulf Coast wholesale jet fuel topped out the same day at $4.705 per gallon, its highest price since April 2022. Wholesale began to ease after the Sept. 15 high, but retail continued to climb through the end of the month.

Figure 1. Jet A Price Change by FAA Region, Aug. 31 – Sept. 30

100LL Avgas: A new high as gains slow

100LL's September national average of $7.59 is up 8 cents from August, setting a new high, though only 4 cents above the July 2022 peak of $7.55.

From Aug. 31 to Sept. 30, every FAA region's 100LL rose between 12 and 24 cents with a standard deviation of 4 cents. These month-end snapshots capture late-month movement that the national monthly average smooths out, explaining why regional gains outpaced the national average's 8 cents. The Southern region's 100LL saw the largest gain, up 24 cents, with Alaska close behind. Unsurprisingly, Alaska remains the highest-priced region for avgas, with a live average of $11.61 at the time of writing. Aside from brief dips, Alaskan 100LL has climbed steadily in 2026, rising $1.80 since January.

The national average for 100LL has not seen a meaningful monthly decline all year. However, gains have started to slow. After rising 37 cents in April, 34 in May and 19 in June, 100LL gained just 13 cents combined from July through September.

Jet A: Third record high of 2026

When people say shoot for the stars, they really aren't talking about fuel prices. At $7.99, September's national average for Jet A set its third record high this year alone. That is 74 cents higher than a previous peak in 2022, but only 6 cents higher than the last high set this May. The national average for Jet A has exceeded 100LL's for the past seven months. September's average was also nearly 28 percent higher than a year earlier.

We are entering October with a live national average of $8.26 at the time of writing, well above September's average Jet A price.

Over the same Aug. 31 to Sept. 30 window and as depicted in Figure 1, every FAA region's Jet A price rose as well. Regions averaged a 36-cent increase with a standard deviation of 15 cents, though the rise was not uniform. Notably, the New England, Eastern, Southern, Southwest and Great Lakes regions rose between 42 and 59 cents. The Northwest Mountain, Central, Alaskan and Western Pacific regions rose between 16 and 27 cents. This past August, we saw a far more uniform gain across the country (standard deviation of 4 cents).

Prices in four of the five fastest-rising regions started climbing in early September. Meanwhile, those in the Great Lakes region and the lower-increase group largely held flat until mid-month.

It is worth watching U.S. diesel exports. The White House denied a Sept. 23 report of a planned 90-day export ban, and Energy Secretary Chris Wright has warned such a ban could raise jet fuel prices. Jet A and diesel are both middle distillates, so changes around one could affect the other.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel: Premium holds above $2

Blended SAF continued to follow Jet A trends, rising 23 cents to a national average of $10.23 in September. That is 6 cents lower than May's high of $10.29.

Over the same window as Jet A and 100LL, every FAA region reporting SAF prices rose between 19 and 77 cents, and the patterns of increase mirror the regional split under Jet A.

GlobalAir.com SAF reporting became substantial enough for analysis in 2023, and since then, the novel fuel has held a premium of roughly $2 or more over Jet A. That premium peaked at $2.99 in February 2024 and has gradually narrowed since, ranging from $2.42 to $2.71 in 2025, then $2.02 to $2.57 so far this year, with September at $2.24.

The Big Picture: Retail is playing catch-up

Every fuel type rose in every FAA region that reports it, but not at the same pace. For Jet A and SAF, most regions with the largest increases started their climb in early September, while the rest held mostly steady until mid-month. 100LL, by contrast, rose more uniformly across the country.

We're not out of the woods yet. Retail continued to climb after wholesale peaked in mid-September, so even if supply disruptions disappear tomorrow, relief may take a while to reach every ramp.

Top Performing Airports

South Bend International Airport (KSBN) in South Bend, IN

title: NorSAF and Nova Pangaea Technologies to develop waste biomass-to-SAF supply chain
description:
NorSAF has agreed to collaborate with Nova Pangaea Technologies to develop an advanced ethanol production plant in Latvia to supply NorSAF’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility.
The project will use locally sourced wood waste to make ethanol using Nova Pangaea’s proprietary technology.
Over the coming decade, SAF production must scale up dramatically.
Approximately 85% of Europe's SAF feedstocks already come from overseas, with China alone accounting for 61%.
The resulting locally sourced ethanol can then be converted into SAF through the alcohol-to-jet pathway as part of NorSAF’s planned SAF production.
text:
NorSAF has agreed to collaborate with Nova Pangaea Technologies to develop an advanced ethanol production plant in Latvia to supply NorSAF’s sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) facility. The project will use locally sourced wood waste to make ethanol using Nova Pangaea’s proprietary technology.

The partnership aims to address Europe’s growing challenge of meeting increasing demand for SAF while developing more resilient and locally sourced feedstock supply chains.

Over the coming decade, SAF production must scale up dramatically. Under EU regulations, aviation fuel suppliers are required to sharply increase the share of SAF at EU airports, rising from 2% in 2025 to 6% in 2030, and jumping to 20% by 2035.

While Europe manufactures a significant portion of its current SAF domestically, production relies heavily on Hydroprocessed Esters and Fatty Acids (HEFA) technology. Meeting regulated targets with this method requires importing vast quantities of feedstocks like used cooking oil. Approximately 85% of Europe's SAF feedstocks already come from overseas, with China alone accounting for 61%.

Although production capacity is technically on track to meet near-term goals in 2030, doing so with overwhelming reliance on imported feedstocks like Chinese used cooking oil threatens supply chain security. As demand accelerates, Europe must secure sustainable feedstocks that are locally available and independent of fragile overseas trade networks. Agricultural and forestry residues present strong regional alternatives, particularly in countries like Latvia, where these bio-resources are abundant. Tapping into this potential requires advanced SAF plants, such as NorSAF, which harness innovative technologies to produce high-performance aviation fuels from alternative local feedstocks.

Nova Pangaea’s REFNOVA® technology converts waste biomass, such as woody and agricultural residues that are plentiful in Latvia, into ethanol and biochar, a valuable co-product which permanently captures carbon and makes the whole process carbon negative. The resulting locally sourced ethanol can then be converted into SAF through the alcohol-to-jet pathway as part of NorSAF’s planned SAF production.

Janis Kisiels, founder and Board Member of NorSAF, said: “Europe cannot strengthen its energy security simply by reducing fossil-fuel imports. We also need to build the industrial capacity to produce the clean fuels that will replace them. Right now, Europe is dangerously dependent on overseas feedstocks like used cooking oil, leaving our aviation sector vulnerable to international supply chain shocks. By tapping into Europe’s own abundant waste resources, particularly those available in the Baltic region, we can build a resilient, domestic supply chain from the ground up. Our partnership with Nova Pangaea is a crucial milestone in developing that strategic capability right here in Latvia, ensuring our future SAF production is sustainable, secure, and locally anchored.”

Jonathan Wood, CCO of Nova Pangaea, said: “This strategic collaboration will ensure we have carbon-negative ethanol to feed NorSAF’s SAF project, using locally sourced biomass waste. This is a blueprint for the type of partnerships we need to scale SAF production in Europe and all regions of the world, enhancing energy security, building a new domestic industry that generates jobs and economic growth while reducing fossil-fuel emissions. According to the International Air Transport Association (IATA), there is sufficient waste biomass available in Europe to produce enough SAF to meet Europe’s ambitious SAF targets for 2050.”

text:
Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul met Airbus executives on Friday to discuss the expansion of investment and technology transfer in Thailand and the development of sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using Thai agricultural products.

Mr Anutin met with Wouter van Wersch, Airbus executive vice-president for international affairs, and Bert Porteman, a representative of Airbus Thailand, at Government House.

The talks focused on expanding cooperation in aviation, space technology, human resources development and clean energy.

The two sides also discussed the development of the aviation industry’s related services, including cooperation with Thai Airways International, as well as workforce development to support industry expansion and the government’s goal of making Thailand a regional aviation hub.

The prime minister said the government was committed to promoting the aviation industry and other future industries.

He praised Airbus for its long-standing cooperation with Thailand in job creation, skills development and support for the country’s aviation sector.

He asked Airbus to consider expanding its existing cooperation and adapting successful models it uses in other countries for Thailand.

This would allow the country to benefit more from Airbus’s global knowledge, technology and networks including its plans to set up a Centre of Excellence in Thailand as a hub for developing knowledge, technology and skilled personnel.

The centre is expected to connect Thailand with Airbus’s global network and provide Thai workers with opportunities to develop advanced technology skills.

On clean energy, the PM proposed that Airbus support the use of SAF produced in Thailand using agricultural materials and production as part of the supply chain.

The use of SAF would help reduce greenhouse gas emissions from aviation while creating new markets, increasing the value of agricultural products and generating additional income for Thai farmers.

Mr Anutin also said Thailand’s cooperation with Airbus could extend beyond aviation. The cooperation would focus on technology and knowledge transfers and human resources development to strengthen Thailand’s capabilities in space and related technologies.

The premier proposed expanding cooperation in space technology and security, building on existing links between Airbus and Thai agencies, including the Geo-Informatics and Space Technology Development Agency (Gistda) and Thaicom Plc.

By helping travelers reach some of America’s most iconic national parks, DAL can encourage them not only to explore these destinations but also to support their long-term protection.

The initiative gives Delta customers, SkyMiles members and employees practical ways to contribute. The introduction of mileage donations through SkyWish is a particularly accessible option, while planned airport experiences and hands-on volunteer opportunities could help turn awareness of conservation into direct involvement.

The partnership also reflects the growing expectation that travel companies consider tourism’s impact and long-term legacy. National parks welcome hundreds of millions of visitors each year, making efforts to preserve their landscapes, infrastructure and accessibility increasingly important as demand for outdoor experiences grows.

Delta’s sustainability strategy, which focuses on fleet efficiency, operations and sustainable aviation fuel, adds another dimension to the partnership. While aviation itself presents environmental challenges, conservation initiatives can complement broader efforts to make travel more responsible.

Ultimately, the collaboration brings together two aspects of the travel experience—the journey to a destination and the responsibility to care for it. If the partnership succeeds in creating lasting opportunities for travelers and employees to support national parks, it could help strengthen the connection between exploration, appreciation and conservation.

Moreover, Delta Air Lines is strengthening its European network with new nonstop routes from Detroit, Boston and Austin to destinations including Athens, Venice and Paris. The expanded Boston-Italy schedule and extended seasonal routes give travelers more options beyond the peak summer period, reflecting Delta’s continued focus on transatlantic connectivity and year-round travel demand.

Apart from Delta Air Lines, many other carriers, including American Airlines AAL and Alaska Airlines ALK, have recently made commendable efforts to expand their network.

American Airlines’ new codeshare partnership with STARLUX Airlines expands U.S.-Asia connectivity, giving travelers easier access to Taipei and other destinations across Asia through 20 major U.S. cities. The partnership offers the convenience of single-ticket itineraries and through-checked baggage, while plans for reciprocal frequent-flyer benefits will provide additional flexibility. By combining American’s extensive domestic network with STARLUX’s growing transpacific presence, the agreement creates more travel options and smoother connections for passengers.

Alaska Airlines’ launch of seasonal nonstop service between San Diego and Loreto marks an important network expansion, giving travelers a new direct connection to Baja California Sur while reaching its 50th nonstop destination from San Diego. Combined with complimentary Starlink Wi-Fi, its 40th-anniversary initiatives and plans for a major new lounge in 2028, the service reinforces the airline’s long-term commitment to the San Diego market while expanding travel options for both leisure and business passengers.

text:
Fuel pump with renewable biodiesel. (Smith Collection/Gado via Getty Images)

A bipartisan bill aimed at boosting U.S. biodiesel production was introduced Sept. 30, with supporters arguing it would provide stability for smaller producers.

The legislation, sponsored by Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.), would extend the Small Agri-Biodiesel Producer Credit through 2029. The credit is scheduled to expire at the end of December. It provides a federal income tax credit of 20 cents per gallon for the first 15 million gallons produced by qualifying small agricultural biodiesel manufacturers.

Kurt Kovarik, vice president of federal affairs for Clean Fuels, a trade association representing biodiesel, renewable diesel and sustainable aviation fuel producers, said the extension would provide certainty for small manufacturers.

RELATED: Oil prices steady as U.S. pressures Europe on diesel

“Small biodiesel producers are making an outsized contribution to America’s energy security right now, producing lower-cost, drop-in distillate fuel that’s needed to keep the economy moving,” Kovarik said Sept. 30. “These companies are investing in rural communities, creating and preserving jobs, and running full-out to provide cleaner, better, more affordable fuel to meet today’s demand.”

The bill follows separate bipartisan legislation introduced in the House in 2025 and reintroduced in 2026 that would extend the Biodiesel Blenders Tax Credit. That measure would continue a $1-per-gallon biodiesel tax credit through 2029 after it expired in 2024.

American Trucking Associations told Transport Topics that it supports both measures.

Some biofuel industry groups contend that increased biodiesel production could help offset higher fuel costs for commercial trucking. Diesel prices have climbed sharply this year, most notably after the U.S. and Israel in February launched a military campaign against Iran; for the week of Sept. 28, diesel cost, on average, $6.382 a gallon, up about $2.63 from a year ago.

The proposed extension also comes amid uncertainty in the biofuels industry. Biofuel groups pushed back against small-refinery exemptions announced by the Trump administration in September under the Renewable Fuel Standard for 2025.

title: A race behind the F1 race: How logistics and banking come together to power the Grands Prix
description:
The resulting new triple-header added new complexities to opera tions for DHL, F1’s official logistics partner since 2004.
If any of these shipments do not arrive on time, it could spell disaster for the Singapore Grand Prix and subsequent F1 races.
The last time an F1 race was cancelled abruptly because of geopolitical tensions was the Russian Grand Prix in 2022, following the country’s invasion of Ukraine.
F1 teams have increasingly turned to ocean freight to cut costs in recent years, Gregory shared, as transport expenses fall under the sport’s cost cap that limits team spending to help level the playing field.
With F1 targeting net zero by 2030, sustainable logistics has become an increasing priority for both racing teams and DHL.
text:
SINGAPORE – Right after this weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Sepang, Malaysia, a fleet of about 200 to 300 trucks will cross the Causeway to Singapore in a race against time.

The Formula 1 race, originally scheduled for April 10-12, was abruptly cancelled along with Saudi Arabia’s after the US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28.

This sudden change meant that DHL had to reshuffle its operations, ensuring all the freight that would have travelled from Japan to the Middle East would now be delivered to Miami in the US for the next race in May, and nothing would be missed out in all the ensuing havoc.

Then, in late July, it was announced that the Bahrain Grand Prix would be staged at the Sepang circuit in Malaysia, slotted in on the Oct 2-4 weekend between the Azerbaijan and Singapore races.

The resulting new triple-header added new complexities to opera tions for DHL, F1’s official logistics partner since 2004.

Not only did the company now have to redirect the F1 teams’ shipments from Baku to Sepang in two to three days, but it will also have to arrange for the transportation of cargo from Bahrain to Malaysia, and move some of the existing equipment already in Singapore by land.

If any of these shipments do not arrive on time, it could spell disaster for the Singapore Grand Prix and subsequent F1 races.

‘Mission-critical’ operation

Each season involves moving around 1,400 tonnes of race cars, engines, fuel and hospitality materials across five continents for 20-plus races,

F1 is a massively complex global operation that runs like clockwork and requires an exceptional level of logistical planning.

The travelling circus can have as little as a few days of turnaround time before the next Grand Prix, and it could very well be in another continent. This means any kind of logistical disruption, like a race car not arriving on the grid owing to a delayed shipment, could have severe repercussions for a Grand Prix.

Thankfully, such instances are extremely rare, said Praveen Gregory, chief executive of DHL Global Forwarding for Singapore, Malaysia and Brunei, in an interview with The Straits Times.

Planning for the global operation begins once the F1 calendar for the new season is announced, typically around the middle of the year.

Each team has multiple sets of equipment travelling around the world on separate logistical routes to reduce wait times and reduce the risk of disruptions.

Throughout the season, the logistics operation would be leapfrogging the race calendar to ensure that every time the F1 contingent arrives at the next destination, everything is already set up and all the necessary equipment from the race that had just ended is now on the way to the following Grand Prix.

“It’s not very often that you read in the news about a race that did not happen because the engine or the tyres were not in place. So it is mission-critical – if we don’t deliver, then the race does not happen. And we have to make our supply chain so resilient that we never fail.”

In 2026 , however, the Middle East conflict threatened to derail the season before it even began.

The last time an F1 race was cancelled abruptly because of geopolitical tensions was the Russian Grand Prix in 2022, following the country’s invasion of Ukraine.

DHL did not comment on the total cost of its F1 logistics, or the cost increase as a result of the last-minute changes in the F1 calendar, though some estim ates say each team spends around US$8 million ( S$10.2 million ) to US$10 million on logistics in a season.

Gregory said the costs are dynamic and dependent on the urgency of teams’ needs and numerous variables, which are constantly changing throughout the season, including changes in shipping routes due to geopolitical developments.

The closure of Middle East airports and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have driven up costs, as DHL has had to rely on other airlines that were also raising their rates. And with fuel among DHL’s largest expenses, it has seen overall business costs rise 10% to 20% because of the surge in oil prices.

F1 teams have increasingly turned to ocean freight to cut costs in recent years, Gregory shared, as transport expenses fall under the sport’s cost cap that limits team spending to help level the playing field. Ocean freight would usually take around 25 to 30 days to travel from Europe to Asia, but with the Middle East conflict disrupting shipping lanes and ships also bypassing the Suez Canal, F1 teams may have to wait twice as long now for their cross-continent shipments, he said.

Sustainability partners

James Nesbitt, Standard Chartered’s managing director and head of global subsidiaries for Singapore and ASEAN, described DHL’s F1 operations as more than just a movement of physical goods, but also a large-scale operation moving money and information.

Behind the scenes, StanChart supports cross-border payments in different currencies and advises on trade compliance.

“Physical flows will always trigger the financial flows. Everything moves smoothly because there is the movement of information between partners, so that money and goods can move... This is the whole ecosystem functioning as an orchestra to bring F1 to life,” said Nesbitt.

Recent protectionist measures like newly imposed tariffs have made trade finance more complex and costly to navigate. For instance, teams may pay more for cargo shipments like merchandise to the US, and American teams like Haas could also incur additional costs importing components.

Just as F1 teams have to make real-time, split-second decisions based on track data, DHL and StanChart have to respond swiftly to sudden changes in country regulations and interest rates that could increase the logistics operator’s costs, to ensure that the F1 operation can run without a hitch, the two executives noted.

StanChart is both a DHL customer and its longstanding banking partner, with the relationship also extending to the area of sustainability.

In 2011, it became the first bank to adopt the logistics group’s GoGreen service, a carbon-offsetting scheme that channelled customer surcharges on shipments into certified environmental-protection projects.

In 2024, the two firms signed a new GoGreen Plus partnership where StanChart would help DHL to scale the use of sustainable aviation fuel, including by absorbing the incremental cost of sustainable aviation fuel used by DHL for the shipment of the bank’s documents. The bank estimates that it would save 3,780 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent between 2024 and 2030.

StanChart achieved net zero in its own operations in 2025 for Scope 1 and 2 emissions, and aims to be net zero in its financed emissions – investment and lending activities – by 2050.

DHL also aims to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050. As its air freight accounts for around 90% of its carbon footprint, sustainable aviation fuel is a key solution to helping it cut emissions.

Gregory said sustainable aviation fuel, which has 80% lower lifecycle emissions than conventional aviation fuel, accounted for about 10% of DHL aircraft’s total jet fuel consumption in 2025, higher than any airline in the world.

DHL also uses sustainable marine fuel for ocean freight, though supplies remain limited.

Gregory noted that while the price of sustainable fuels has fallen over the past five years, they remain a costly alternative and will become comparable to regular fuels only as increased demand drives higher production.

With F1 targeting net zero by 2030, sustainable logistics has become an increasing priority for both racing teams and DHL.

Gregory said F1 has long been a test bed for automotive technology, and DHL’s sustainability partnership with the sport could similarly inspire its customers. While awareness and conversations about sustainability have grown among Asian companies, they are still largely unwilling to spend on such initiatives, he noted.

The way DHL is moving F1’s cargo “in a high-speed, highly agile environment in a fully sustainable manner” shows that sustainability can be achieved even when speed is of the essence, he said, calling it a good case study for others to learn from or replicate.

Nesbitt said StanChart’s sustainable aviation fuel partnership with DHL could result in more opportunities to help South-east Asian countries and companies transition effectively from carbon-based business models to a pure-play sustainable finance model, tapping the bank’s cross-border expertise and its extensive relationship with the logistics firm.

This would allow companies to focus on channelling capital into inherently low-carbon businesses or assets like renewable energy developers, instead of only taking steps to decarbonise.

Noting that there is often “a vacuum of leadership” in the world of sustainability, he added: “Instead of waiting for our clients to ask us to reduce costs or push a sustainability agenda, we have to get ahead of this and play a role in delivering against the sustainability goals.”

text:
The Cardano Foundation and Petrobras are developing a blockchain system designed to make fuel sustainability data verifiable and reduce reliance on fragmented documents, databases, and manual data reconciliation.

The Cardano Foundation and Brazilian state-owned oil and gas company Petrobras unveiled 2 projects built on the public Cardano blockchain to verify fuel sustainability data. The solutions cover sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) and Diesel R renewable diesel, enabling related environmental data to be traced from source documents through final use.

The sustainable aviation fuel project is being developed by Petrobras, the Cardano Foundation, and Ledger Labs at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-Rio). SAF is considered a lower-carbon alternative to conventional aviation fuel, but its use requires reliable verification of the environmental benefits being claimed.

One issue with the existing system is that certificate data can be stored across separate documents and databases maintained by producers, airlines, and other participants. This complicates audits and creates a risk that the same environmental benefit could be counted more than once.

The project addresses this issue through a Book-and-Claim model, which separates the accounting of a physical batch of SAF from its associated environmental attributes. This allows the environmental benefit to be assigned to an airline, an organization, or an individual passenger regardless of where the fuel was produced and used.

The process consists of 5 main stages:

An SAF certificate is verified for compliance with CORSIA requirements and other recognized standards.

The verified certificate is converted into standardized digital tokens containing data on a specific volume of fuel.

The tokens are distributed to airlines or allocated to passenger trips based on the route and calculated emissions.

Passengers can claim and redeem tokens through a dedicated application, receiving a certificate that includes their name, route, distance, and number of tokens.

Once the environmental attribute is claimed, the corresponding tokens are permanently removed from circulation on the blockchain, preventing their reuse.

Each verified SAF certificate is tokenized on the public Cardano network. CS-SAF tokens are used to represent the fuel’s environmental attributes. Their metadata can include the amount of fuel, batch identifier, CORSIA data, and a reference to the source data. The tokens can be issued, transferred, and verified. Once used, they can be permanently removed from circulation.

The second project involving Petrobras and PUC-Rio focuses on Diesel R, Petrobras’ renewable diesel fuel. In this case, the Cardano network links data generated at different stages of the process, including fuel production, transportation, and use.

The goal is to create a continuous digital record of the product’s life cycle. This approach could simplify verification of Scope 3 indirect emissions data, since accounting for these emissions depends on information from multiple external participants across the supply chain, including suppliers, carriers, and other companies.

Both projects create a unified, verifiable chain of records that doesn’t depend on fragmented documents and information systems. For SAF, the distributed ledger connects the original certificate to the tokens and the final claim of the environmental attribute. For Diesel R, similar infrastructure is intended to provide data traceability throughout the fuel’s life cycle.

description:

text:
By: CATHERINE WATKINS, Hydrocarbon Processing

Hydrogen's (H2’s) reality check: the money is flowing, the offtake isn't. At the 16th Dii Desert Energy Leadership Summit in Istanbul, producers, engineers, buyers and shippers agreed that hydrogen technology is ready, but the bottleneck is bankable demand, and the first real market may be the refinery.

Five years ago, H2 panels were about ambition. Now, the "Hydrogen Reality Check" session at Dii Desert Energy's summit was about execution. Chaired by Dan Feldman, Global Head of Energy at King & Spalding, the discussion brought together Air Products Qudra, Masdar, thyssenkrupp Uhde, Smartenergy, SEFE, Kawasaki Heavy Industries and Fraunhofer ISE. Their shared verdict: the sector has moved from announcing gigawatts to financing them, and the hard part now is commercial, not technical.

The money is real. Dr. Faye Al Hersh, Associate Director, Development UAE at Masdar, anchored the discussion in the Hydrogen Council's new Global Hydrogen Compass 2026. Committed clean H2 investments have reached $130 B, with 6.9 MMtpy of capacity across more than 570 projects that have passed final investment decision (FID). Operating capacity grew 70% in a year to approximately 1.7 MMtpy.

The drivers are shifting too. The Compass finds that energy security, resilience and industrial growth now match or exceed decarbonization as the main rationale in most regions with committed investment.

The host country was candid about the pace. Opening the summit, YEO Technology Chairman and CEO Tolunay Yıldız said H2 progress has been slower than many hoped: costs remain high, and buyers and investors need regulatory frameworks and long-term commitments. He still backed green H2 for hard-to-electrify industries and pointed to Turkey’s target of 5 GW of electrolyzer capacity by 2035.

Bankability is the bottleneck. Fatemah Din, Senior Vice President MENA at thyssenkrupp Uhde, put it plainly: the challenge is no longer the technology. It is bankability, long-term offtake agreements and stable regulation. What the market needs now, she argued, is success stories measured not in gigawatts announced but in FIDs reached, gigawatts contracted and infrastructure built.

Al Hersh described the mismatch at the heart of the problem. Buyers of ammonia, methanol and sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) are used to small, short-term contracts, while lenders want long-term offtake before they finance a renewable power plant. Mandates help only when they bite: without penalties, a mandate simply sets the price of non-compliance. She added that EU rules are being transposed unevenly by member states, with refining emerging as the first-mover sector, with wider industry lagging.

Sebastian Budischin, Senior Vice President Business Development at SEFE, spoke from the middle of the value chain. “Producers approach SEFE as the natural offtaker,” he said, “but its own industrial customers struggle to commit long term amid volatile markets and shifting rules. No single company can carry the full market risk of a 10-plus-yr contract for 100,000 tpy, so risk has to be shared along the whole chain.” He warned that if everyone waits for someone else to move first, the industry will be having the same conversation in a few years.

Christian Pho Duc, CTO of Smartenergy, added that H2 only works as part of a wider system of flexibility, storage and gas-grid links, and that offtake demand is strongest where regulation creates a clear obligation.

Follow the refiners, and the pipes. Ebubekir Koyuncu, CEO of Blue Hydrogen Industrial Gases (BHIG) and CEO of Air Products Qudra, offered the most pragmatic view. Market conditions have changed since the industry's early giga-scale bets, and Air Products has adapted by looking for partners and "low-hanging fruit." With refiners earning strong margins, the near-term business is supplying refinery and industrial gas customers, including through what he described as a major H2 pipeline network under construction in the Middle East. “Offtakers,” he said, “remain overwhelmingly price-driven: without mandates or penalties, few will pay a premium for green molecules.”

That puts infrastructure center stage. Panelists agreed that common-user infrastructure (CUI), meaning shared pipelines, storage and export terminals, can de-risk giga-scale projects that no single developer could justify alone. Al Hersh said Masdar's early projects rely on existing infrastructure and pointed to Egypt and Morocco as markets where government-led infrastructure models are taking hold. See urged that shared infrastructure be treated as an enabler, not left to become the bottleneck. She also noted that cheaper solar and batteries are raising electrolyzer utilization and improving project economics.

On carriers, MENA Hydrogen Alliance Chairman Frank Wouters interviewed Eiichiro Miyazoe, Managing Director of Kawasaki Heavy Industries Middle East. Kawasaki is scaling up from the 1,250-m³ Suiso Frontier, the world's first liquefied H2 (LH2) carrier, to a 40,000-m³ vessel ordered by Japan Suiso Energy for demonstration by FY2030. Its boil-off gas will fuel a H2 dual-fuel generator. Kawasaki is also working with EcoLog on an LH2 import terminal at the Port of Amsterdam. Wouters argued that LH2 is often undervalued: liquefaction energy is spent where power is cheap, no cracking is needed at the destination, and large liquefiers are far more efficient than today's small units.

A silk road for eSAF. Wouters also presented the work of Dii's eFuels task force, making the case for Türkiye as a "Silk Road" for SAF. The ingredients are there: a global aviation hub, a national airline operating > 500 aircraft, a 120-GW solar and wind target he expects to be exceeded, and a H2 strategy targeting production costs below $2.40/kg by 2035. Because aircraft bought today will fly for decades, drop-in fuels are one of the few levers aviation has.

He outlined three proven routes:

Power-to-liquid via Fischer-Tropsch

Methanol-to-jet (with methanol made where power is cheap and upgraded in refineries)

HEFA from used cooking oil.

Demand signals are stacking up, from ReFuelEU's requirement of 70% SAF by 2050, including 35% synthetic fuel, to ICAO's CORSIA from Jan. 1, 2027. Türkiye's existing refineries with jet capacity are an asset. The task force's asks to policymakers include early-mover protection against rule changes, more flexibility on CO₂ sourcing until direct air capture matures and multipliers in support schemes.

The long view. Prof. Dr. Christopher Hebling, Director International at Fraunhofer ISE, closed the session with perspective. He showed a 1912 newspaper article warning that coal burning could warm the climate "in a few centuries." The science was right, he noted, but the timing was not: the effects are being felt now, with global emissions approaching 40 Gt of CO₂/yr. Energy transitions have historically been additive, and fossil fuels still supply roughly 80% of primary energy. Even so, solar deployment is now measured in hundreds of gigawatts a year, and research into natural hydrogen and negative emissions is opening new options.

Hebling ended where the panel began: no one succeeds alone. He credited Dii's summit as the kind of platform where research, industry, policy and finance meet and new projects are formed. On the evidence of this session, hydrogen's next chapter will be written less by technology breakthroughs than by who agrees to share the risk.

H2Tech is a supporting partner of the 16th Dii Desert Energy Leadership Summit.

text:
German energy group Uniper has signed a capacity reservation agreement for future sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) production from Syzygy Plasmonics’ NovaSAF facilities in Central and South America.

The supply will be produced using Syzygy’s proprietary Rigel photocatalytic reactor, which converts regional biogas feedstocks into low-carbon jet fuel.

The deal strengthens commercial support for Syzygy’s lead project, NovaSAF-1 in Uruguay, which is currently approaching a final investment decision (FID).

German energy company Uniper has entered into a capacity reservation agreement with deeptech developer Syzygy Plasmonics to secure future output from planned NovaSAF production facilities across Central and South America.

The agreement covers sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) produced via Syzygy’s proprietary Rigel photocatalytic reactor technology, which processes regional biogas streams into synthetic fuel.

The deal provides crucial commercial backing as Syzygy prepares for a final investment decision (FID) on its flagship NovaSAF-1 project in Uruguay.

Because Syzygy’s production pathway supports compliance with both biogenic and Renewable Fuels of Non-Biological Origin (RFNBO) standards, the deal provides Uniper with flexible, dual-certified supply to meet European aviation mandates under ReFuelEU Aviation and CORSIA.

The capacity reservation aligns with Uniper’s strategy to expand its low-carbon fuel trading desk, positioning the energy major to fulfill rising airline demand for compliant SAF across European hubs.

“Uniper’s decision to reserve NovaSAF capacity reflects the commercial traction our platform is attracting at the moment when it is most needed to meet mandate volumes,” said Trevor Best, CEO of Syzygy Plasmonics.

“Agreements like this affirm that the market is moving to meet EU commission targets.”

By leveraging photocatalytic reforming rather than traditional thermal conversion, Syzygy aims to significantly lower the unit production costs and operational emissions associated with processing distributed biogas into drop-in fuels.
